- **The origin is the belt's spawn edge, not the spawner's position.** Measured from the belt, so a designer who moves the spawner in Studio does not shift every number; and so every body shares one origin instead of being measured from its own birth point.
- **The frame is the belt's own** (`PointToObjectSpace`), with the belt's **half-length added back** because the transform measures from the geometric centre. The half-length is read from the part's `Size.X`, not hard-coded as `28`, so a re-sized belt keeps the origin on its real edge.
- **`0` means safest, and the sort is ascending.** The elimination edge is `+X`, so the body nearest death has the *largest* number. This is the paragraph the code now carries, because a leaderboard sorted by "distance travelled" looks right and puts the loser first.

**The `LEADER_IS_FURTHEST_FROM_THE_EXIT` flag is gone.** It existed to make the direction reversible while the question was open; the question is answered, and a two-mode constant around a decided fact is a maintenance surface. The reasoning lives in `collect()`'s docblock and in the field's own docblock instead.

**The column shows a unit now.** `${math.floor(distance)}st` rather than a bare integer: an unlabelled number in a leaderboard column reads as a score, and this one grows while a racer loses. Whole studs rather than a tenth, because the value moves at roughly `BALL_SPEED_DECAY_RATE` studs a second and decimals would change on every broadcast without adding information.

**Everything else from item 124 stands unchanged** - the flip, the queue for mid-animation payloads, the five-row scroll, the `hudCore` placement, the gold self ring, the owner-id-based "previous order", and the `userId`-in-payload decision that replaces the brief's `isMe`.

**Audit.** `src/server/services/leaderboard-service.ts` (sign, origin, sort comparator, `beltGeometry` accessor replacing `beltFrame`), `src/shared/leaderboard.ts` (`distance` docblock), `src/client/controllers/leaderboard-controller.ts` (`formatDistance`). Build, lint, prettier and tests green at 289; `\uXXXX` zero; `flamework.build` unchanged since item 124 (still 23 identifiers).

**Studio-only:** that `0st` at the top of the column reads as "best" to a player without a legend, and that the body that gets eliminated first is visibly last by a growing number rather than by position alone.

## 126. `0st` was not a broken suffix - it was a distance wearing an ordinal, and there was no rank column at all

**Reported as "the rank starts at 0 and always says `st`".** Half right, and the half that was wrong matters: **there was no rank on the board.** The number in the right-hand column was `distance` - studs from the spawn edge - and the previous round had suffixed it with `st` so it read `0st`, `15st`, `23st`. So the two symptoms had one cause each: no place was ever displayed, and a distance was dressed as one.

**Fixed by giving the rank its own column and taking the unit off the distance.**

- **`getOrdinal` in `src/shared/ordinal.ts`**, with `ordinal.spec.ts` pinning the boundaries: `1st`, `2nd`, `3rd`, `4th`, `11th`-`13th`, `21st`-`23rd`, `101st`, `111th`-`113th`, `121st`, plus a float and a zero case. It lives in `shared` rather than inline because it is arithmetic with boundaries, and boundaries are the thing that gets "simplified" later - `11` ending in `1` is exactly the case a one-digit rule gets wrong.
- **The rank is `index + 1`**, written in `commitOrder` from the row's position in the *ranked* list. That is the one line the first build would have got wrong had it published a rank at all: a Lua array is 0-based, a place is not.
- **The distance column lost its suffix** and is now a bare count. It is not a place, and it must not look like one.
- **`RANK_WIDTH = 28`** in a fixed column, so the name starts at the same x on every row rather than shifting by a digit.

**One build defect from the previous round surfaced and is fixed.** `UIListLayout.AbsoluteContentSize.ToString()` was a no-op - the property returns a `Vector2` that roblox-ts discards, so the "force a layout solve" line compiled to nothing and was a type error besides. The FLIP no longer needs a solve: **the travel distance is derived from the change of index**, `(oldIndex - newIndex) * (ROW_HEIGHT + ROW_GAP)`, which is exact because the rows are uniform by construction - the divider lives *inside* the container so it cannot change the pitch. Measured `First`, derived `Last`, tweened `Invert -> Play`; it is still FLIP, without a frame yield or a property read whose value nobody wants.

**Audit.** New: `src/shared/ordinal.ts`, `src/shared/ordinal.spec.ts`. Modified: `src/client/controllers/leaderboard-controller.ts` (rank label, name column shifted, distance formatter, derived FLIP delta, `IsA` guard on the divider). **295 tests in 21 files** - six new assertions. Build, lint and prettier green; `\uXXXX` zero; `flamework.build` unchanged at 23 identifiers.

**Studio-only:** that `28` pixels is enough for `12th` in the caption size without eliding, and that a two-column row still reads left-to-right as place, name, distance.

## 127. The publisher was dead, not empty - a roblox-ts loop lowering bug, plus "any ball" instead of "any owner"

**Reported as "No players" on the board.** The board was not showing nobody; it had **never received anything**, because the service's publisher thread died on its first `Playing` tick and a `task.spawn` thread that throws is gone for the session. The one line that survived was `leaderboard-service:196: attempt to index nil with 'distance'`.

**The bug is in the compiled Luau, not in the TypeScript.** `for (let index = 0; index + 1 < ordered.size(); index++)` is lowered by roblox-ts to `for index = 0, #ordered - 1` - one iteration too many at every size, and at size `1` it runs once with `behind = ordered[2] = nil`. With one body on the belt (a solo playtest, before the debug spawn key was pressed) the first tick threw. Two fixes, both kept:

- **The bound is spelled out and the degenerate case returns early**: `if (ordered.size() < 2) return ordered;` then `const lastIndex = ordered.size() - 1; for (let index = 0; index < lastIndex; index++)`. The compiled output is now a `while`-shaped loop with no arithmetic in the header, so the lowering has nothing left to get wrong.
- **Each tick is `pcall`ed** and a failure logs `[Leaderboard] tick failed, retrying next interval`. A HUD must not be killable by one bad frame, and a dead publisher that prints once is the worst possible failure mode: it looks exactly like "there are no players".

**"Any ball", not "any owner".** The ranking now includes **every live body** the round tracks, not only those carrying an owner identity. The old filter was defensible for the winner rule and wrong for a HUD: it produced an empty board on a solo playtest and excluded exactly the bodies a designer adds while testing. Bodies with an owner are named after the owner; the rest fall back to their own instance name (a `decoy` twin reads as `Decoy`). The winner rule is still `RoundService`'s business and is untouched - an ownerless body can appear in the standings and still not compete, which is the asymmetry the `decoy` power is built on.

**That required re-keying the payload on the body rather than the owner.** `LeaderboardEntry` gained `key` (the body's full name - unique within a round, stable for the life of the body) and `userId` became `0` for "no owner" rather than an absent field, so the remote never carries a nil hole. The client's row map and its `previousOrder` are keyed by `key`; the self-highlight now tests `userId > 0 && userId === LocalPlayer.UserId`, which stops `0` matching anybody.

**Audit.** `src/shared/leaderboard.ts` (entry shape), `src/server/services/leaderboard-service.ts` (pcall, widened source, keyed ranking, spelled-out bound), `src/client/controllers/leaderboard-controller.ts` (payload parsing, keyed rows, self test). Build, lint, prettier and tests green at **295 in 21 files**; `\uXXXX` zero; `flamework.build` unchanged at 23 identifiers.

**Studio-only:** that a five-row board mixing players, `Debug#N` bodies and decoys reads sensibly, and that pressing the debug spawn key now fills it within one second.

## 128. The single-row bug was `GetFullName()` - every ball is called `Ball`

**Reported: seventeen live bodies, one row on the board.** The row key was `ball.GetFullName()`, and `GetFullName` returns the *path*. All balls are siblings named `Ball` under `Workspace.SpawnedBalls`, so all seventeen reported `Workspace.SpawnedBalls.Ball` - one key, one map entry, one row, overwritten by whichever body the loop reached last. The visible row (`1st Debug#2 16`) was simply the last writer. Nothing was wrong with the layout, the loops or the draw order.

**The fix is a server-assigned key.** `KeyFor(ball)` hands out `B1`, `B2`, ... from a `Map<BasePart, string>` and a counter, cleared with `previousRanked` when the phase leaves `Playing`. It is the only thing here guaranteed distinct, and because it is assigned once per body the client's row identity survives a rank change - a per-broadcast index would renumber every row on every elimination.

**Duplicate names, Part C.** Ownerless bodies are all called `Ball` or `Decoy`, so they now read `Ball 7`, `Decoy 12` - the numeric half of their own key. Stable for the body's life, and it matches the identity the client is using, so two rows that look alike are genuinely different bodies rather than a rendering artefact.

**The cap is gone, not raised.** `LEADERBOARD_ENTRY_LIMIT` is deleted from `shared/leaderboard.ts` and `collect()` returns `ranked` directly, so the payload carries the whole field - at most `MaxLiveBalls` (50) entries of four small fields, once a second. The old rationale ("a fifty-row HUD is a wall of text") was wrong for this game: the player is watching every body on the belt, and a five-row window hid the racers in front of them.

**The client shows every row and scrolls.** `TOP_ROWS` - which was a *cap* - became `VISIBLE_ROWS`, a **viewport height**, and `displayList` (top five plus a pinned self row) is deleted; the pinned-row machinery goes with it, including the divider child and `isPinned`. The list is a `ScrollingFrame` with `AutomaticCanvasSize.Y`: the box is five rows, the canvas is however many exist, so a fifty-body round scrolls inside a fixed-height panel instead of pushing the board off the screen.

**One latent bug found on the way.** `commitOrder` is what writes `LayoutOrder` **and the rank text**, and it only ran on the sliding path. A row created on a broadcast whose order had not changed would therefore sit at order `0` with an empty rank column until something else moved. Both non-slide paths now commit as well, with a comment saying why the call is not redundant.

**Audit.** `src/shared/leaderboard.ts` (cap constant deleted), `src/server/services/leaderboard-service.ts` (key map, names, uncapped return), `src/client/controllers/leaderboard-controller.ts` (scroller, no display cap, no pin, commit on every path). Build, lint, prettier and tests green at **295 in 21 files**; `\uXXXX` zero; `flamework.build` unchanged at 23 identifiers.

**Studio-only:** that the scrollbar is legible at `4` pixels over a charcoal face, and that seventeen rows of `Ball 3`, `Decoy 7`, `Debug#12` read as a race rather than as a debug dump - if the labelled bodies dominate, the next step is hiding ownerless rows again behind a toggle rather than a hard filter.

## 129. A decoy twin now reports its parent's identity, so the board no longer outs the fake

**Reported: the leaderboard revealed the decoy by naming it `Decoy 12`.** Right, and it is worse than cosmetic - the whole `decoy` power rests on a twin being indistinguishable, and the one UI that lists every body was naming it.

**`BallSpawnerService.ownerIdentityFor(ball)` answers "who does this body represent".** It reads the body's own owner pair first; failing that it walks `decoysByParent` to find a parent whose twin this is and returns the *parent's* identity. The leaderboard calls it and uses the result for both `userId` and `name`, falling back to the old `${ball.Name} ${key.sub(2)}` only when neither exists.

**The reverse lookup is a scan, not a second map.** `decoysByParent` is keyed by parent, so finding a twin's parent means walking its values - at most one entry per lane. `forgetDecoy` already argues the same way for its own reverse pass ("the map is at most one entry per lane, which is why the reverse scan is a loop rather than a second index that could disagree with the first"), and ~40 iterations once per body per second is cheaper than an index that can rot after a missed delete.

**The winner rule is untouched, and the comment says why.** `RoundService` decides who competes from `OwnerUserId` **on the body**; `ownerIdentityFor` is a display question that writes nothing. A twin reporting its parent's identity on the leaderboard is still an ownerless body everywhere the simulation looks - which is exactly the separation items 77/79 built.

**The client needed no changes, and that was verified rather than assumed.** Rows are keyed by `entry.key` (`Map<string, Row>`), `removeNotIn` keeps a `Set<string>` of keys, and `orderChanged` compares keys - nothing dedupes by name or by `userId`, so two rows carrying the same player's identity render as two rows. The highlight tests `userId > 0 && userId === LocalPlayer.UserId`, so **the owner sees both their real body and their twin ringed in gold**, while everyone else sees two unmarked `Player1` rows. That asymmetry is the power working.

**Where the brief was wrong, in one place.** It says a debug ball is an example of a body that should return `undefined`. Debug bodies are *owned* - synthetic ids `-1`, `-2`, ... with `Debug#N` display names - and `hasOwnerIdentity` accepts them deliberately, so they return their own identity and keep their names on the board. `undefined` is only reached by a body with no owner and no live parent: a stray, or a twin whose parent has already been destroyed (in which case there is no lookalike left to protect).

**Audit.** `src/server/services/ball-spawner-service.ts` (`ownerIdentityFor`, `identityOf`, `hasOwnerIdentity` import), `src/server/services/leaderboard-service.ts` (spawner injected, identity from the spawner, three now-dead attribute imports removed). No client change. Build, lint, prettier and tests green at **295 in 21 files**; `\uXXXX` zero; `flamework.build` unchanged at 23 identifiers - no new service.

**Studio-only:** that two identical rows with different ordinals read as "this player has two balls" rather than as a duplicate-row bug, and that the owner's gold ring on both rows is understood as "both of these are mine".

## 130. The white box was `refreshChestButtons` re-opening the hit area

**Reported: the `Open 1` / `Open 10` buttons are pointy and white-ish.** One line caused it, and it had been latent since item 123:

```ts
entry.button.BackgroundTransparency = enabled ? 0 : DISABLED_WASH;   // removed
```

`applyChunkyChrome` makes the button a **transparent hit area** and draws the face and shadow as its children ? it already set `BackgroundTransparency = 1`, so nothing was missing there. This block then wrote a transparency of `0` straight back onto the button, which paints **Roblox's default light grey** (`163, 162, 165`) behind both plates. The plates cover the middle of the cell, so what showed through was the **corners**: a rounded shadow does not cover its own bounding box, and until item 123 the shadow was square and hid the problem. Rounding the shadow is what turned a grey box into pale wedges.

**Fixed by routing the wash through `dimChunkyChrome(entry.button, !enabled)`** ? the same call `applyPolicy` and the purchase guard already use for the Premium buttons. That re-washes the *face* and its *labels*, the only two properties on a chrome'd control that actually draw, and it means **all six buttons dim identically** instead of two of them using this file's own pair of constants.

**Two constants deleted, not left behind.** `DISABLED_WASH` (`0.55`, the plate) and `DISABLED_TEXT_WASH` (`0.35`, the labels) existed only for that block. `dimChunkyChrome` carries one wash (`0.45`) for both, and keeping two locally-tuned numbers beside it is exactly how one button ends up dimmer than another. The three manual `TextTransparency` lines went with them ? `dimChunkyChrome` already walks the face's text descendants.

**Audit: every chrome'd control, and none of them touches a background any more.** Nine `applyChunkyChrome` call sites ? `close`, both chest buttons, ball card, fusion row, fuse button (shop), the picker's card and footer button, and the tab strip. A sweep of every `BackgroundTransparency =` assignment in `src/client/controllers` now returns only frames, labels and the picker's tinted ball; no button. The trap is written into `applyChunkyChrome`'s own docblock so the next caller does not rediscover it: *the button's background must stay at 1, and a caller that writes it re-opens the hit area as a visible plate whose failure mode is pale corner wedges, not a grey box.*

**Audit.** `src/client/controllers/shop-controller.ts` (the wash, two constants, three text-transparency lines), `src/shared/ui/chunky-chrome.ts` (docblock only). Build, lint, prettier and tests green at **295 in 21 files**; `\uXXXX` zero; `flamework.build` unchanged.

**Studio-only:** that a disabled chest button now reads as a dimmed card rather than a dimmed grey slab, and that `0.45` is the right amount for both the face and its two lines ? the old pair was `0.55`/`0.35`, so the plate is slightly more transparent and the text slightly less.

## 131. Debug key `2` spawns the auto-bots itself

**Reported: pressing `2` in a one-player Studio session still ends the round instantly.** Correct - `forceWaiting` spawned the *players*, and a single competitor is the same thing as `last standing`, so `Waiting` counted down into a `Playing` phase that the first tick closed. The workaround was to press `4` inside a `WAITING_SECONDS` window, which is a race against a timer, not a harness.

**The gate in `debugSpawnCompetitors` now accepts `Waiting` as well as `Playing`.** The original reason for refusing everything else stands and is untouched: a body in a phase with no tick is an orphan. `Waiting` is not that phase - it is the phase that already spawns the players' own bodies, `enterPlaying` is on a scheduled timer from it, and `Intermission`/`PostGame` stay refused (neither has a scheduled entry into `Playing`, and `Intermission` wipes every body on the way in). Bots spawned during `Waiting` behave exactly like the player's body: `spawner.setRoundActive(false)` and `setBeltSpeed(0)` mean they sit still through the countdown, then are raced, eliminated and cleaned up by the same code in `Playing`.

**Placement: after `startWaitingRound`, before `enterWaiting`.** Both halves matter. After, because `startWaitingRound` rolls the offers and spawns the players - a spawn ahead of it would take spawner slots first and the human body would arrive second. Before, because `enterWaiting` prints the transition and arms the countdown, and its `competitors=` figure is read off the argument, not off the world.

**`debugSpawnCompetitors` now takes a reason and returns a count, and both exist for the log.** Without the count, `enterWaiting(reason, spawned)` would print `competitors=1` beside a round holding five bodies - a log that disagrees with the world is worse than no log, and that number is the one a reader uses to decide whether the round was worth watching. Without the reason, the line could not distinguish an intentional `4` from the automatic pair, and the two are the only way to tell whether the fix is doing anything. The debug remote call site ignores the return value, which TypeScript allows; `print` keeps the ASCII hyphen in `not Playing or Waiting` rather than the file's arrow glyph.

**Audit.** `src/server/services/round-service.ts` only - `forceWaiting` (the call and its comment), `debugSpawnCompetitors` (signature, guard, refusal log, success log, `return spawned.size()`), and its docblock, which swapped the "refused outside `Playing`" argument for the `Waiting`-is-safe one plus a "why it returns a count" section. Build, lint, prettier and tests green at **295 in 21 files**; `\uXXXX` zero; `flamework.build` unchanged at 23 identifiers - no new service and no decorated method, so nothing reflection-visible changed.

**Studio-only:** that the bots-plus-player population is right for watching a round with - there is no `DEBUG_COMPETITORS` constant, the press spawns one per **bound spawner** (`getBoundSpawnerCount()`), so "four" is a property of the place rather than a number this round chose, and that the extra `[Round] debug spawn (auto-bots for debug key 2)` line between the spawn and the transition reads as one press rather than as two.

## 132. Rounds pay coins, and the payout gets its own visual language

**Reported: there is no way to earn coins.** Correct, and worse than cosmetic - the chest, the picker's re-roll and the fusion verb all spend a currency whose only sources were the command bar and a Robux purchase. A round now pays **base 10 for turning up plus 15/10/5 for the podium**, granted through the `grantCoins` path item 51 wrote and nothing had ever called.

**The rule is `shared/round-payout`, not eight lines in `endPlaying`.** `RoundService` cannot be constructed in Jest (its dependencies reach `DataStoreService`), so a payout written inside the transition would only be checkable by playing a round - the argument that produced `round-outcome`. Eleven assertions now cover the table, the reversal, the no-winner branch, synthetic owners and duplicates.

**Placement is the elimination record, read backwards.** There is no ranking in this game: a round ends on "one competitor left wins", the `initialLiveCount` guard was deleted with item 72, and the leaderboard is a 1 Hz snapshot of live distances with hysteresis on top. So `RoundService` records the order bodies leave (in `settleEliminations` and in `handleExternalDestruction`, the two places an owner is read) and the winner is prepended. **A `no survivors` round ranks nobody and pays base only** - the alternative was promoting whichever body a cleanup loop happened to destroy last into first place, which the banner would then contradict.

**The participant list is recorded at `trackBall`, and it had to move twice.** First at `enterPlaying`, which was wrong for a reason item 131 created: competitors are spawned during `Waiting` (including the auto-bots), so a reset at `Playing` entry would have paid nobody. It now lives in `clearAllBodies`, the one place every round's body set ends.

**Where the brief was wrong, in four places.** (1) It asks the client to read `Coins` before and after the grant; `grantCoins` publishes the new balance *before* the remote fires, so "before" no longer exists when the handler runs - both numbers travel in the payload. (2) Its `{ base, bonus, total }` payload cannot drive a rolling balance for the same reason. (3) "Wait 3 seconds" after counting up does not fit: `POST_GAME_SECONDS` is 5, the wipe that ends the phase is drawn above this panel's layer, and fade-in + two counts + a roll + 3 s of hold is ~6 s, so the cover would cut the counter mid-roll. The hold is now **derived** from the phase. (4) `initialLiveCount` does not exist to calculate from.

**The panel is a new direction, and it is local on purpose.** `shared/round-payout` is shared, but the look is not: `payout-controller` owns its own palette (`#D4AF37` gold, near-black glass at 0.1 transparency, one 1 px gold hairline) rather than `chunkyDarkTheme`, because a payout is a statement about money and the chunky language belongs to things you press. It mounts on the `splash` layer - above the HUD, below the wipe. The fade is **one `NumberValue`** driving every element as `mix(1, resting, reveal)`, so "revealed" is a single fact and the fade-out is the same tween reversed; the counts and the balance are `TweenService` on `NumberValue`s read through `Changed`, not `RenderStepped` loops that would need disconnecting on a self-destructing frame.

**Audit.** New: `src/shared/round-payout.ts` (+ `.spec.ts`, 11 assertions), `src/client/controllers/payout-controller.ts`. Changed: `src/server/services/round-service.ts` (participant/elimination records, `recordElimination`, `payOut`, `createRoundPayoutRemote`, `readCoins`), `src/shared/remotes.ts` (`RoundPayout`), `src/server/services/economy-service.ts` (one stale docblock line: `grantCoins` said "not called by anything yet"). Build, lint, prettier and tests green at **306 in 22 files**; `\uXXXX` zero; `flamework.build` regenerated to **24 identifiers** (the new controller).

**Studio-only:** that `#D4AF37` on near-black is the intended read rather than "brass", that the derived 3 s hold is long enough to read the breakdown, that the panel survives a phone's viewport as a centred card, and that the coin grant is visible in the shop's pill at the next `Intermission`.

## 133. The payout panel was a stranger: it now speaks Chunky, and only its paint changed

**Reported: the payout screen looks like a bank, not like this game.** Item 132 built it from a brief that asked for "sleek fintech" - glass at `0.1` transparency, a 1-pixel gold hairline, GothamMedium at caption weights - and the result was internally consistent and wrong, because **visual identity is a contract**. A payout is one of the most-seen surfaces in the game and the player meets it seconds after a round ends, which is the exact moment the game should look most like itself.

**The paint came across; the motion did not move one line.** The reveal `NumberValue`, the three counting `TweenService`s, the derived hold, the `formatCoins` roll and the self-destructing frame are the same code as item 132. A style is a set of colours, weights and offsets, and none of those are animation decisions - so the restyle is confined to what is *drawn*.

**The face is `buildChunkyPanel`, not a copy of its hierarchy.** The shadow depth (`10`), the face-only outline (`6`), the corner radius (`12`) and the centring anchor come from the module the store and the inventory already use; a copy here would be a second description of the house style that drifts the first time either is retuned. The face colour is `theme.paint.panel`, which the theme documents as *equal to* `CHUNKY_PANEL_FACE` - named through the theme so a sheet retint reaches this panel. **The shadow plate is left at the module's `CHUNKY_PANEL_SHADOW`**, and that is the one place the brief's "use the theme for the face and shadow colours" could not be followed: the theme has no shadow-plate slot, and `colors.shadow` is pure black - darker than the `10, 10, 12` outline the builder draws on the face, which would erase the very band that creates the depth.

**A hairline rule cannot survive this language, so the divider became a plate.** The fintech panel separated the balance with a 1-pixel gold line; hairline rules are the one thing Chunky never draws. Bands are separated here by a **value step** - `paint.surface`, one step below the face, with its own `rgb(20, 20, 20)` outline at the control weight - which is the same move the store's bands make and reads as inset rather than raised.

**The bar became a well.** `4` pixels with no edge became `16` with `paint.trough` behind it and `CHUNKY_CONTROL_STROKE` outlines on both the trough and the fill, so an empty bar still reads as a slot cut into the panel and a half-full one reads as a solid object sliding in it. The `Size.X` tween is untouched.

**The text outlines had to join the fade, and that is the one bug the restyle could have shipped.** A `UIStroke`'s transparency is its own property - lowering `TextTransparency` does not fade the outline with it, which is exactly why `elimination-splash-controller` tweens a word and its stroke as two targets. Every label is now built through one `label()` helper that pushes the stroke `outlineText` created onto the same driver list, so the reveal is still one number and no glyph outline is ever visible without its glyph.

**Where the brief was wrong, in three places.** (1) `scale.ts` exports **one** font, `FONT` = GothamMedium; there is no GothamBlack to import from it. GothamBlack is the family's *display* weight and lives as a local constant in `chunky-button` (`TITLE_FONT`) and a local literal in `leaderboard-controller`, so it is a local `TITLE_FONT` here too - adding a second export to `scale.ts` would be a second answer to "what font is this game". (2) The store's `coinDot` has **no** stroke: it is a flat `20`-pixel circle in `colors.coin` with a `UDim(1, 0)` corner, because it sits inside a saturated price pill. The size and the colour here are the store's own; the 2-pixel `colors.shadow` edge is added because this coin sits on charcoal next to the largest number on screen, and that difference is deliberate rather than a copy. (3) "The 3-second hold must remain exactly as it is" - it does, and it is *derived*: `5 - 0.2 - 1.25 - 0.35 - 0.2 = 3.0`, so the note is satisfied by construction rather than by a literal.

**Audit.** `src/client/controllers/payout-controller.ts` only. No server change, no payload change, no new controller - `flamework.build` is unchanged. Build, lint, prettier and tests green at **306 in 22 files**; `\uXXXX` zero.

**Studio-only:** that the derived 3 s hold still reads as a pause rather than a stall under a heavier panel, that GothamBlack at `18` does not crowd the title row, and that a `3`-pixel outline on a `16`-pixel bar reads as an edge rather than eating the fill at third place's 33%.

## 134. Round payouts were tuned down, and two time-based rewards went in beside them

**Reported: rounds are the only source of coins, so a session without a win earns nothing.** The placement ladder is now `[10, 5, 0]` - first pays 20 all in, third pays the base rate and nothing more - and two schedules were added: a **50-coin daily login** and a **25-coin stipend every 15 minutes** of play.

**`toStored` was the trap, and the brief never mentioned it.** It names `Profile`, `StoredProfile`, `readStored` and `release` - but `toStored` is the function every *save* builds its value from, so a field it forgets is erased on every single write. Omitting the two timestamps there would not have failed to compile and would not have looked like a bug: the daily login would simply have paid again after any round, chest or admin command, because each of those saves would have written a profile that had never been paid. Both `toStored` and `release`'s rebuild now restate both fields, and `reward-schema.spec.ts` asserts the round trip rather than trusting that the three literals agree.

**`grantCoins` already saves, so the reward is stamped *before* it rather than after.** The brief's sequence - grant, update the timestamp, save - is two `UpdateAsync` calls with a window between them; a crash in that window leaves coins granted and the clock unread, and the next pass pays again. Setting the stamp first puts the balance and the timestamp in **one** write. On failure `grantCoins` reverts the coins and `award` reverts the stamp to the value it captured, so a failed save leaves the reward due rather than silently skipped.

**The playtime condition, taken literally, pays a brand-new player twice.** `os.time() - (lastPlaytimeRewardAt ?? 0) >= 900` is true for the `0` that every migrating profile reads as, so a first join would mint 25 coins in the same second as the 50-coin login and show two toasts for one arrival. `playtimeBaselineAtLoad` moves a stored value that is **already past its interval** forward to the load time, so the stipend means fifteen minutes *of playing*; a stored value still inside the interval is kept, which is what stops a rejoin every fourteen minutes from resetting progress forever.

**Where the brief was wrong, in four places.** (1) `toStored`, above - the write path. (2) The three-step grant, above - it is one step. (3) `lastDailyRewardAt?: number` - optional in memory would put `?? 0` at every reader and make "never paid" two spellings; the repo's own precedent (`purchases`) is required in `Profile`, optional on disk, defaulted in `readStored`. That is a compile error in four existing spec factories, which is the point: the compiler lists the readers. (4) The playtime condition's first-join behaviour, above.

**The ticker is one thread, not one per player.** `PLAYTIME_TICK_SECONDS = 60` wakes a single loop that walks `Players.GetPlayers()` and asks each profile a question: at most a minute of lateness on a fifteen-minute stipend, and nothing to leak. The pass is `pcall`ed because a background thread that throws is gone for the session - one bad profile would otherwise switch the stipend off for everyone. `os.time()` is read once per pass so every player in it is judged against the same instant.

**The toast is its own controller, not the payout panel.** A payout replaces the screen's attention; a toast must not interrupt. It is 240x52, top-centre, slides down one card-height while a single reveal driver fades the face, the shadow plate and six outlines in, holds `3`s, then reverses and destroys itself. **No frame in it is `Active`**, so a reward arriving mid-picker cannot eat a click. Toasts stack by slot rather than replacing each other, because the one thing a notification must not do is silently drop a message.

**Audit.** New: `src/shared/rewards.ts` (+ `.spec.ts`, 9 assertions), `src/server/test/reward-schema.spec.ts` (6), `src/client/controllers/reward-toast-controller.ts`. Changed: `src/shared/round-payout.ts` (ladder + the ratio note), `src/shared/economy.config.ts` (five constants), `src/shared/remotes.ts` (`RewardToast`), `src/server/services/player-data-store.ts` (fields, `readTimestamp`, `toStored`, `emptyProfile`, `release`), `src/server/services/economy-service.ts` (`award`, `startPlaytimeRewards`, `payPlaytimeRewards`, the load hook, the remote), and four existing spec factories for the new required fields. Build, lint, prettier and tests green at **322 in 24 files**; `\uXXXX` zero; `flamework.build` regenerated to **25 identifiers** (the toast controller). `SCHEMA_VERSION` untouched at 1.

**Studio-only:** that a real DataStore round-trip preserves both timestamps (the write path is asserted, the platform is not), that `release`'s rebuild keeps them (it runs inside an `UpdateAsync` transform and needs a live store), that the toast's 52-pixel card does not collide with the topbar on a phone, and that 60-second ticker lateness is invisible in the log.

## 135. The daily-login toast plays on every Studio session, and pays nothing

**Reported: the daily toast is untestable.** It fires at most once per twenty hours, so a playtest either shows it by luck or does not show it at all - and the thing being iterated on is a card, not a balance.

**In Studio, a session that is *not* due now fires the toast anyway, with no grant.** No coins move, no save happens, and `lastDailyRewardAt` keeps its stored value, so the real reward still lands on its real schedule. The log says so explicitly:

```
[Economy] morri reward Daily Login preview amount=50 (studio, no grant)
```

The word is `preview` and the amount is the schedule's nominal value, because the card is being *rendered* rather than reported - a toast that said `+50` after a real grant and a toast that says `+50` in a preview are different events, and the log is the only place that distinction can survive.

**It fires on the read-only path too.** A Studio session whose `DataStore` is refused would otherwise reach `return` before any reward code, which is the state where a designer most wants to look at the toast. Gated on `isStudioSession()` and nothing else, because the whole point is that a plain `Play` shows it without a step somebody has to remember - a debug key would be the same untestability one level down.

**`RunService.IsStudio()` still has exactly one reader.** `player-data-store` documents that rule on `profileKey` ("one read means the namespace cannot be half a namespace"), so rather than importing `RunService` into a second file the predicate was lifted into `isStudioSession()` and `profileKey` now calls it. The audit statement stays true: one environment read, two callers.

**Nothing else changed.** The `.spec.ts` suites are untouched (this is a branch no test can reach - the environment is a fact, not an input), the payload is the same, and the playtime stipend was deliberately **not** given the same treatment: it is minutes away, so it needs no preview.

**Audit.** `src/server/services/player-data-store.ts` (`isStudioSession`, docblock), `src/server/services/economy-service.ts` (`toast` split out of `award`, `previewDailyLogin`, two call sites in `spawnLoad`). Build, lint, prettier and tests green at **322 in 24 files**; `\uXXXX` zero; `flamework.build` unchanged.

**Studio-only:** that the preview toast appears on a plain `Play` with a warm profile and with a refused store, and that the coin pill does not move when it does.

## 136. The paid chest got its own odds table and a guarantee, and the epic row got read wrong twice

**Reported: the faster free track makes the Robux chest feel optional.** Two changes: the paid chest now rolls **65% rare / 25% epic / 10% legendary** (was 75 / 22.5 / 2.5), and the ten-chest bundle **cannot fail to deliver a legendary**.

**The paid chest could not be retuned at all before this, and that is the real finding.** `robuxChestWeights()` did not own a table - it *copied* `RARITY_WEIGHTS` and zeroed commons, with a docblock celebrating the coupling ("make legendaries rarer remains a one-number edit that moves both chests at once"). That is exactly the trap this task needed to escape: changing the paid legendary rate would have changed the **free** chest's, which the brief forbids. So `ROBUX_CHEST_WEIGHTS` is now its own exported table and the function is a per-roll copy of it (a caller holding a shared config table is one stray `weights.legendary = 0` away from a silent product bug).

**The bundle floor forces the last roll; it does not upgrade the worst one.** Upgrading a granted ball means decrementing one count and incrementing another inside the all-or-nothing snapshot - a bug there corrupts `ownedBalls` rather than merely mis-stating a rarity. Taking the last slot keeps the invariant "ten balls, each added exactly once", keeps the first nine rolls at their honest odds, and makes the guarantee a statement about the *set*, which is what the product sells. The rule is a `Rarity` (`ROBUX_CHEST_BUNDLE_GUARANTEE`), not a boolean, so a future "bundle guarantees an epic" is one word.

**Where the brief was wrong, in four places.** (1) It says the weights are `750 / 225 / 25` out of 1000 - they were `300 / 90 / 10` out of 400, because the map was a filtered `RARITY_WEIGHTS`. (2) `ROBUX_CHEST_PRICE_ROBUX` is `30`, not `25`, and the bundle is `250`, not `200`. (3) "Update `odds.ts` tests to match" understates it: `odds.spec.ts` also carried an **invariant** ("beats the coin chest for every tier"), and at least one *other* spec derived the Robux odds from `RARITY_WEIGHTS` - both had to be re-pointed or they would have gone on asserting the coupling. (4) The `economy.config.spec.ts` assertion that the surviving weights sum to *less* than the full table is now false and meaningless: the paid table totals 1000 on its own, so there is no renormalisation step left.

**The docblock was wrong twice before the specs caught it, and both drafts are recorded.** First: "the trade is the epic tier, 25% here against the free chest's 30%". The coin chest's epic rate is `90 / 1000 = 9%`, not the `300` rare weight read as a percentage - so the paid chest wins *every* tier and there is no trade. Second: the "reach tier pays for it" comparison is only true against the *previous paid table* (75 -> 65 rare), not against the free one (65 against 30). The comment now carries a tier-by-tier table plus a note that the first draft was arithmetic on the wrong row, because that is the kind of mistake a table prevents and prose does not.

**The Policy gate is untouched, and should be.** `policyAllowsPurchase` answers "may this player receive a paid random item at all". The floor caps the downside of a draw; it does not make the draw deterministic - the player still does not know which ball, nor which of the ten slots carries the tier - so the item is exactly as random as it was and the disclosure obligations are identical.

**Audit.** `src/shared/economy.config.ts` (`ROBUX_CHEST_WEIGHTS`, `robuxChestWeights`, `ROBUX_CHEST_BUNDLE_GUARANTEE`, the product-id docblock), `src/shared/odds.ts` (docblock only - the function already derives from the weights), `src/server/services/economy-service.ts` (`guaranteed` parameter, `floored` flag, the floor log line, the constant passed at the bundle call site), `src/shared/odds.spec.ts`, `src/shared/economy.config.spec.ts`, `src/server/test/economy-service.spec.ts` (four new bundle-floor cases, including the interaction with the empty-pool abort). Build, lint, prettier and tests green at **327 in 24 files**; `\uXXXX` zero; `flamework.build` unchanged at 25 identifiers.

**Studio-only:** that a real receipt with the bundle product id returns a legendary in ten rolls that would otherwise have none (the roll is injectable and the floor is asserted, but `ProcessReceipt` needs a real purchase), and that the store's odds copy - which reads `robuxChestOdds()` - now prints 65 / 25 / 10 without a second edit.

## 137. The decoys were never enumerated, only *filtered* - and that is why they were still missing

**Reported: decoys are still not on the leaderboard.** Item 128 removed the owner filter, item 129 taught the board to name a twin after its parent, and neither could help, because `collect()` never saw a twin in the first place:

```ts
for (const ball of this.round.getLiveBalls()) {   // RoundService's *tracked competitor* set
```

A decoy is created by the `decoy` power through `spawnDecoy`, never by `spawnRoundCompetitors`, and it is deliberately ownerless - so it is not in `liveBalls` and never was. The board was repaired everywhere except at the door.

**The enumeration is now `CollectionService.GetTagged(TAGS.ball)`**, which is exactly what `clearAllBodies` already uses and for the identical reason: *the tag is how a body says it is in the game; a tracked set is how one service remembers its own spawns.* The second goes stale the moment anything else creates a body - the 21:20 bug that left an untracked ball rolling 274 studs past the belt, and now this one. `spawnDecoy` adds `TAGS.ball` before parenting, so the tag sees it. `RoundService` is still injected, but now only to answer **which phase it is** - never which bodies exist.

**Putting twins on the board exposed a leak, and it is fixed in the same round.** `ownerIdentityFor` answered "who is this twin" by reverse-scanning `decoysByParent` - and `forgetDecoy` deletes that link when the *parent* dies, which is the ordinary end of a decoy's life (the parent is the body being raced). From that instant the orphaned twin would have published as `Decoy B7`, announcing the fake to the whole server. The twin now carries a copy of its parent's `{userId, name}`, taken at spawn in `decoyIdentities`; it survives the parent by design, it is one map read instead of a ~40-entry scan per body per second, and it cannot disagree with anything because it is a snapshot rather than an index.

**A diagnostic, because this is the second "X is missing from the board" that a screenshot had to explain.** One line per round, at the first broadcast:

```
[Leaderboard] round standings: bodies=14 namesShared=1
```

`namesShared` is the number of rows sharing a name with another row - which is what a decoy twin looks like and what nothing else does. A round with `bodies=14 namesShared=0` now *says* the twin is absent instead of leaving it to be inferred from a picture.

**What the pasted log proves, and what it does not.** It shows the twin alive (markers on `Workspace.SpawnedBalls.Decoy`, `bodyTaggedBall=true`, `[Decoy] outline granted decoy=Workspace.SpawnedBalls.Decoy`) while `live=13` competitors were tracked - so the body existed, carried the tag, and had a parent to name it after. The board could not have listed it. What the log cannot show is the broadcast contents; that is what the new line is for.

**Audit.** `src/server/services/leaderboard-service.ts` (tag enumeration, `IsA` guard, `distinctNames`, `reportedRound`, two docblocks), `src/server/services/ball-spawner-service.ts` (`decoyIdentities`, the copy at spawn, the simplified `ownerIdentityFor`, the delete in `forgetDecoy`). Build, lint, prettier and tests green at **327 in 24 files**; `\uXXXX` zero; `flamework.build` unchanged at 25 identifiers.

**Studio-only:** that the board now shows two identically-named rows while a twin is alive (the code paths are asserted only by reading - the spawner and the service both need a DataModel), that losing the parent keeps the twin's row named, and that a decoy's row carries the parent's name rather than `Decoy`.

## 138. Coins make a sound when they arrive, and the toast payload had to learn which arrivals were real

**Extends items 82/83 (the throttle rule), 88 (one event, two effects), 89 (a tuning row per id) and 132/134/135 (the coin sites).** `79302475372626` is now `COIN_SOUND_ASSET_ID`, played by `playCoinSound` from the two places a balance can actually rise in front of a player: `payout-controller` on a `RoundPayout` payload, and `reward-toast-controller` on a `RewardToast` payload.

**The user's belief that the round payout is the earn site is wrong, and the correction is the substance of this round.** `EconomyService.grantCoins` has **two** callers, not one: `RoundService.payOut` (every competitor, base plus placement bonus) and `EconomyService.award` (the daily login *and* the playtime stipend, item 134). All three were silent. The other writers of `coins` are `setCoins` (an absolute admin set that can also *lower* a balance), `applyProfileReset` (`/dev wipeData`), and `emptyProfile`'s `STARTING_COINS` ? all deliberately silent, with the reasons on `playCoinSound`. `applyRobuxChestGrant`, the bundle grant, `fuseBalls` and the chest spend never raise a balance at all: they write balls, or subtract coins, so listing them as "coin writers" is the shape of false positive this enumeration was meant to avoid.

**The preview exposed a real hole in the wire, and the fix is a payload field rather than a client-side guess.** Item 135 fires the *same* `RewardToast` message on every Studio session while granting nothing, and the client had no way to tell the two apart ? `RunService.IsStudio()` would also silence the real daily login in a playtest, and comparing the balance before and after races replication. `RewardToastMessage` now carries `preview: boolean`, set `false` by `award` and `true` by `previewDailyLogin`; the card draws either way and the **sound** is gated on it. The validator requires the field rather than defaulting it, so a payload that lost it cannot become a sound for money that did not move.

**Unthrottled, and it is the purchase sound's precedent rather than the elimination sound's.** A payout is one grant per round per player (fired once from `endPlaying`, which returns unless the phase is `Playing`); the daily is one per twenty hours; the stipend one per fifteen minutes. `canPlay` here would be a third gate behind schedules that are already the gate, and on the day one of them changed it would *hide* a double grant instead of letting it be heard. Item 134's `playtimeBaselineAtLoad` is what keeps the daily and the stipend from landing in one second ? the double *sound* the double *grant* fix also removed ? and that is the one sentence the throttle decision needed. A payout and a stipend *can* still coincide (the tick does not look at the phase, roughly one round in nine hundred); both play, because two real grants are two events.

**`/dev setCoins` stays silent, deliberately.** It is an admin verb rather than an earn, it can lower a balance as easily as raise one, and it has had no client signal since item 65 ? adding a remote whose only job is to tell a client an admin moved its coins would be a new channel opened for a debug path. The shop's coin pill already moves, which is the feedback an admin needs.

**No `now` parameter, unlike the throttled three.** Nothing on this path reads a clock; a `now` would be passed and discarded, and the two existing unthrottled players (`playClickSound`, `playPurchaseSound`) take only the player for the same reason. The seam that matters is `play`, which is what the specs count through.

**The spec pins the literal three times and that is on purpose.** `sounds.config.spec.ts` asserts the bare id, its `rbxassetid://` rendering, and the tuning row ? matching the existing pattern for the hit and pickup ids ("one digit is all that stands between a sound and silence"). The *application* code contains it once, in `sounds.config.ts`; `grep` over `src/client` and `src/server` finds zero. `sounds.spec.ts` gains two cases: eleven calls at one instant produce eleven plays (the anti-re-throttle assertion), and an elimination immediately afterwards still plays, proving the coin sound never writes `lastPlayedAt`. That second probe uses `999`, deliberately below the elimination block's `1000`, because this spec runs in file order against module state and a later stamp would break its neighbour ? a trap worth the comment it now carries.

**Audit.** `src/shared/sounds.config.ts` (id, tuning row, three docblocks re-counted), `src/shared/ui/sounds.ts` (`playCoinSound`, two docblocks), `src/shared/rewards.ts` (`preview`), `src/server/services/economy-service.ts` (`toast` takes `preview`), `src/client/controllers/payout-controller.ts`, `src/client/controllers/reward-toast-controller.ts` (sound + validator), `src/shared/sounds.config.spec.ts`, `src/shared/ui/sounds.spec.ts`. Build exit 0, lint 0 problems, prettier clean, `\uXXXX` zero. **`npm test` was not run** ? this session was told not to drive Studio ? so the new cases are written, reviewed for the module-state ordering trap above, and unexecuted.

**Studio-only:** whether the id resolves to audio at all, whether `0.8` reads right against the payout panel (the two fire together and are meant to match), and whether the coin sound and a same-frame payout/stipend collision sound like two events or one louder one.

## 139. The round has music: one `Sound` with a lifetime, looped by arithmetic because the engine's loop replays the intro

**Extends items 82/83 (what is throttled and why), 88 (one event, two effects), 89 (a tuning row per id, and `soundFor` as the one construction site), 138 (the last sound round, and the four-document habit this round keeps).** Deliberately does **not** touch the six event players: nothing in this round adds a `play<Thing>Sound`, and their throttle rules are unchanged.

**The lifecycle is a new module, `src/shared/ui/song.ts`, and `soundFor` was split rather than duplicated.** The song is the first sound in this tree that is *owned*: started, its `Volume` tweened, its `TimePosition` moved, and destroyed at the end of a phase. Reusing the cached instances `PlayLocalSound` copies would have meant destroying a cache entry and mutating a `Volume` that the next copy inherits. So `buildSound` is now exported as the one construction-and-tuning site and `soundFor` is a cache layered on top of it ? **the rule is preserved, not relaxed**: `shared/ui/sounds`, `shared/ui/song` and nothing else build a `Sound`.

**`Looped = false`, and the wrap goes to the intro's end rather than to zero.** `Sound.Looped` loops `0 -> TimeLength`, which replays the intro every 82 seconds ? audible, permanent, and invisible to every build, log and test except the pure one in `song.spec.ts`. The typings declare `Sound.LoopRegion`, `Sound.PlaybackRegion` and `Sound.PlaybackRegionsEnabled`, which is *probably* the engine-native answer, but they give the signature and not the semantics (whether the first pass starts at `LoopRegion.Min` and skips the intro, or plays from `0` and only loops inside the region), and guessing wrong is silent in both directions. The arithmetic stays and the successor is named in the docblock.

**The fade-out cannot start before the end, and this is the round's one genuine impossibility.** Item 37 gave `Playing` no time cap and made its end a property of `checkEndCondition` at the instant "one competitor remains" becomes true ? so *neither side* knows the round is about to end, and "start the fade two seconds before it does" names a moment nobody can compute. The two requirements it implies (a two-second fade, silence at the transition) cannot both hold. What is built: the fade starts when the client observes `Playing -> PostGame`, and the song is silent and destroyed **~2.1 s into `PostGame`** ? a deliberate musical tail under the payout panel rather than a hard cut on the frame. A server remote fired at `endPlaying` would buy ~100 ms (the replication hop) and not a single frame more.

**A dropped-frame guard nearly shipped a bug that skips the intro.** The first draft had `songWrapTarget(timePosition, playing)` re-seat the playhead whenever `playing` was false, to cover a frame landing past the clip's end. But a `Sound` whose asset has not loaded reports `IsPlaying = false` **and** `TimePosition = 0` ? so that branch would have seeked to `0:05` on every frame of the load and opened the song with the intro missing, which is the exact failure the loop-point constants exist to prevent. The predicate is now one number, `started` gates the frame loop, and the stopped case is left to `Sound.Ended`, which fires on real completion and never on a pending load. The wrong version is kept as a spec case so it cannot come back.

One connection, disconnected in `destroyNow` and nowhere else ? `destroyNow` is the only exit, including the fade's own completion, so there is one disconnect site and no path that forgets it. The fades are tweens because a tween is owned by the instance it drives and dies with the `Sound`; a per-frame `Volume` write would be a second connection to disconnect on four different paths.

**The restart replays the intro, and the reset hard-cuts.** `Playing -> Playing` (debug key 3, item 38) destroys the handle and builds a new one from `TimePosition = 0`, `Volume = 0` ? no crossfade, because that is two songs at once. `Playing -> Intermission` (debug key 1) destroys immediately: the round was abandoned rather than finished, and a two-second outro over a lobby would be music for a round that no longer exists.

## 140. The arena has a `motionBlur` overlay, and its two rules are a pure module because the interesting bug needs three phases

**Extends items 84/85/86 (the VFX pattern: recursive find, two refusals, inert clone, `CFrame` before `Parent`), 95-101 (the trail siblings and the one-scale lesson), 111 (`Rate` as a tweened value) and 139 (destroy-and-recreate on a `Playing` entry).** Deliberately does **not** touch `windBoost`, `tailWind`, `hitEffect` or the ball phantom: those are per-ball and attribute-driven, this is per-phase, and no attribute was added.

**One clone of `ReplicatedStorage?motionBlur`, at the `EliminationZone`, alive only during `Playing`.** Every emitter's authored `Rate` is captured at clone time, zeroed, and ramped back up over `MOTION_BLUR_FADE_SECONDS` (0.5 s); leaving `Playing` ramps it to 0 and destroys the tree when it arrives. `Enabled` is only ever used as an off-world guard ? disabling an emitter at fade-out start drops its live particles on that frame, which is a cut, not a fade.

**The zone reader matches `RoundService.findZone` and therefore refuses a `Model`.** The brief asked for a `BasePart`-or-`Model` branch; `findZone` is `GetTagged(TAGS.eliminationZone)` filtered to `IsA("BasePart")` with a live parent, so a tagged model eliminates nobody today. Supporting one here would be a second, quieter reading of the same tag, drawing an arena effect around a boundary the round does not use. Playing` fits inside that window (a debug key does it in one press). ## 141. The blur moved to the front of the zone, and the anchor became a function

**Reported: "it's kind in the middle of the `EliminationZone`. Please put it to the front."** Correct ? item 140 placed the clone at `zone.CFrame`, which for a `Part` is its **geometric centre**, so the effect read as a haze hanging over the arena instead of entering it.

**The placement is now the zone's `-X` face, composed in the zone's own frame.** `motionBlurAnchor(zoneFrame, zoneLengthStuds)` returns `zoneFrame.mul(new CFrame(-(length / 2) + MOTION_BLUR_INSET_STUDS, 0, 0))`. Front is `-X` because that is the tree's own belt convention (`+X` toward the exit and elimination, `-X` the front and the spawn edge) and the same axis `isInsideZone` measures a body against ? one definition, two readers, no second coordinate system.

**Why an offset from the fixture and not an absolute `x = 0`.** The brief's coordinate is a position in whatever frame the reader happens to be holding; this names a position *relative to the zone*, so moving the fixture in Studio moves the effect with it and resizing the zone keeps the effect on the face rather than buried somewhere inside. `MOTION_BLUR_INSET_STUDS` (0) is the one knob if the effect should sit a little back from the face.

**Rotation is carried through deliberately, and it is the opposite of item 97's rule.** A ball trail must ignore the body's rotation and stay parallel to the ground; this effect belongs to a hand-placed fixture and should lie along **it**. If the zone is rotated in Studio, the effect rotates with it.

**Five new assertions, and one of them caught my own arithmetic.** `motion-blur.spec.ts` now pins the front face, that `Y`/`Z` do not move, that the anchor follows a moved zone and a resized one, and that the zone's basis is preserved. The rotation case was written as `Z = -25` on the assumption that local `-X` becomes world `-Z`; the Y-rotation matrix's first column is `(cos, 0, -sin)` = `(0, 0, -1)` at 90 degrees, so `-20` along that is `(0, 0, +20)` and the answer is `15`. Corrected before build, and the derivation is now in the comment rather than left as a number.

## 142. The blur kept the zone's rotation: the clone now takes the asset's, and item 141's argument is corrected in place

**Reported: the effect renders at the wrong angle although the asset was rotated in Studio.** Item 141 composed `clone.CFrame` out of the zone alone, so the zone's basis replaced the asset's ? and its docblock argued for that ("rotation is carried through deliberately, and it is the opposite of item 97's rule"). That argument had one sound premise and one wrong conclusion: a fixture gives a stable **position**, and it has no opinion about which way a **particle asset** was drawn. Only the asset knows that, and it says so with its `CFrame`.

**The composition is item 97's, on a fixture instead of a body.** `motionBlurCloneFrame(zoneFrame, zoneLengthStuds, assetRotation)` returns `new CFrame(anchor.Position).mul(assetRotation)` ? position from the zone's front face, rotation from the asset. `assetRotation` is captured **once at boot**, after both refusals, beside the resolution (item 97 captures `windBoost`'s the same way, for the same reason: the asset does not change between rounds).

**The two wrong spellings are both still wrong, and the spec says so.** `anchor.mul(assetRotation)` and `anchor.Rotation.mul(assetRotation)` each compose the **zone's** basis into the asset's, so a zone turned 90 degrees turns the effect 90 degrees further. The negative assertion (`the clone's basis is NOT the zone's`) is the half that catches a "simplification", because with an unrotated asset *and* an unrotated zone all three spellings agree.

**`motionBlurAnchor` is unchanged and its basis is still load-bearing.** The offset is composed in the zone's local space, which is what puts the position on the correct **face** of a turned box; the clone just no longer inherits that rotation. Its docblock is rewritten in place rather than deleted ? the old sentence is the trap, and a reader who only saw the fix would not know why a fixture's rotation was ever thought to matter.

**`ToOrientation()` is not XYZ, and that is the one factual correction to the brief.** The typings are explicit: *"approximate angles that could be used to generate `CFrame`, if angles were applied in Z, X, Y order (Equivalent to `toEulerAnglesYXZ`)"* ? so it is YXZ-applied and returns **radians**. The boot field prints `math.deg` of those three in the engine's own `x,y,z` order, one decimal place, because the whole point is comparison with a `Part`'s `Orientation` box in Studio. The helper is named and docblocked rather than inlined, because "degrees" is one word and "the order is not XYZ" is the trap.

## 143. The face is a boundary, not a place: the blur moved to a fifth of the way in, and the depth became proportional

**Reported: "the effect appears outside the box, at the front."** That is exactly what item 141 bought. It placed the clone on the front **face** of the zone - which is the *boundary* itself - so the origin sat on the wall and the emitters sprayed outward from there. A point on a boundary divides its own cloud in half, and the half outside reads as a pane hanging in the air in front of the arena.

**Third position, and the first one with a reason that survives being written down.** Item 140 put it at `zone.CFrame` (the centre - "a haze over the arena"). Item 141 moved it to the front face (the boundary - "outside the box"). This one places it **`MOTION_BLUR_DEPTH_FRACTION = 0.2` of the zone's length in from the front face**: far enough that the effect belongs to the arena, near enough the front that it does not become the all-over haze item 140 was fixing.

**The depth is a fraction, and that is the substantive change.** `MOTION_BLUR_INSET_STUDS = 0` was an absolute studs offset, which fixes *one* zone size and needs re-deriving the moment the fixture is resized - because what has to stay inside is a share of the box, not a distance. The fraction travels with the fixture: `motionBlurDepthStuds()` is the one definition of the resolved depth, so the anchor and the log cannot disagree about how far in it went.

**`depth=` joined the `show` line, because this number is the one being tuned.** The position alone is unreadable without knowing the zone centre; `depth=8` says in studs exactly how far inside the front face the effect sits, which is the quantity to raise if the cloud still pokes out and lower if it sits too deep.

**The spec's hand-computed values were all recomputed, not just the ones that failed.** Every anchor case moves: `88` replaces `80`, `238` replaces `230`, `70` replaces `50`, and the rotated-zone case `Z = 7` replaces `15`. The clone-frame cases move with them (`Z = 12`, `X = -2`), because they assert positions taken from the anchor. The rotation assertions are untouched - item 142's rule is unaffected by depth.

## 144. The red wedge is an invisible collider behind a camera-facing sprite that spins when it is taken

**Extends items 42/45 (the pickup's placement and why it is where it is), 76/80 (the consume decision and the `recycle` pad), 90/91 (the re-touch measurement this round's throttle reuses), and 85 (recursive asset resolution).** Deliberately does **not** touch `onPickupTouched`, `pickupDecision`, `speedAfterPickup`, or the pickup sound's own throttle - the collection path is byte-identical, and only the body's appearance and the client's rendering changed.

**The body is now a `Block` with `Transparency = 1`.** `PICKUP_SIZE` is unchanged, so the bounding box is the wedge's old box; the *contact* volume grows by the half of the box the wedge's slope left empty, which is the forgiving direction. `Anchored`, `CanTouch = true`, `CanQuery = false` are all unchanged, and **`CanCollide` was already `false`** - the brief said the wedge was collidable, and a collidable pad would be a wall across a lane. `Color`, `Material` and `Shape` writes are gone with `PICKUP_COLOR`, which is deleted rather than left as a constant with no reader.

**The visible half is a `BillboardGui` the client builds, not a `ParticleEmitter` with `FacingCameraWorldUp`.** `FacingCameraWorldUp` is an `Enum.ParticleOrientation` value and only an emitter can consume it - and an emitter cannot ease a quad to rest at a chosen angle. Its only rotation inputs are a constant `RotSpeed` and a per-particle random `Rotation`, neither of which is an `Exponential`/`Out` spin, and standing one up means emitting continuously to keep one static picture on screen. A billboard faces the camera natively, stays upright (its roll follows the camera's up, which for this chase camera is world-up to within a few degrees - the behaviour `FacingCameraWorldUp` names), and exposes `ImageLabel.Rotation`, a tweenable number.

**The spin is one tween of `ImageLabel.Rotation` to `from + 360`, accumulated rather than reset.** A fixed `0 -> 360` target would make a second spin a no-op; resetting to `0` after completion would snap the sprite backwards on the frame the tween ends. The effective duration is `math.max(PICKUP_SPIN_SECONDS, PICKUP_SPIN_VISIBLE_SECONDS)` - one number, floored so a later "make it snappier" edit cannot cut the cue below the time it takes to notice.

**The client needs no knowledge of `recycle`.** A consumed pad is destroyed on the server, which destroys the billboard parented to it; a `recycle` pad survives, so the sprite simply stops spinning and goes static. **The survival is the signal** - nothing in the sprite controller reads a power.

**The `Touched` caveat is written down rather than papered over.** Balls are pinned server-owned and pads are anchored, so this contact is simulated on the server; a client `Touched` for a contact it did not simulate is not guaranteed to fire, and when it does it can trail the collection by a frame or two. The state is accepted, not solved: the two fixes available are a server-fired cue (a new remote, which the brief rules out) or a per-frame overlap scan (a constant cost to rediscover what the physics engine already computed). **If playtesting shows no spin at all, the answer is the server cue - not a longer tween.**

**The image resolves from either a Studio instance or the id, and the boot line says which.** A `Decal`/`Texture`/`ImageHandleAdornment` named `pickupSprite` anywhere under `ReplicatedStorage` supplies the `ContentId`; otherwise `PICKUP_SPRITE_ASSET_ID` does, with the `rbxassetid://` prefix written in the one place the id is consumed (the `soundUri` argument). Both inputs end as one string on one `ImageLabel.Image`, so this is two *sources*, not two render paths - and the asset's class could not be confirmed from here, which is exactly why both are accepted.

**Every "triangle" in the pickup path was rewritten.** `PickupService`'s class docblock, its `live` field, `clearPickups`, `onPickupTouched`'s three references, `positionFor`, `PICKUP_SIZE`'s docblock, `PICKUP_SPAWN_INTERVAL_SECONDS`'s, `PICKUPS_FOLDER_NAME`'s, `attributes.ts`'s "the one thing only a triangle is supposed to cause", and three README lines all said triangle. The comment that argued *for* the wedge is rewritten in place rather than deleted, because half of its reasoning (a part picked for how it looked) is the assumption this round removed.

**Audit.** New: `src/client/controllers/pickup-sprite-controller.ts`. Changed: `src/server/services/pickup-service.ts` (the body, the import, twelve prose fixes), `src/shared/tuning.ts` (six new constants, `PICKUP_COLOR` deleted, three prose fixes, region renamed), `src/shared/attributes.ts` (one word), `README.md` (three lines). Build exit 0, lint 0 problems, prettier clean, `\uXXXX` zero, `flamework.build` regenerated to **28 identifiers**. **`npm test` not run**, per the standing instruction.

## 145. A billboard's `Size` is two different properties in one value, and the sprite was fed the wrong one

**Extends item 144 (the sprite this repairs) and item 143's method: a number that came from engine documentation rather than from the typings still has to be checked against what the engine *did*.** Item 144 listed the size question as unverified — "whether a billboard's offset `Size` reads as studs (engine documentation, not the typings)" — and it was the one claim in that round that was wrong. The playtest report was "can't even see it, there are only blue-ish dots": the sprite existed, was parented to the pad, carried the right image, and was **2.6 pixels across**.

**The bug is a `UDim2` component, not a number.** A `BillboardGui`'s `Size` is not a `GuiObject`'s `Size`. The engine's own guide (`ui/in-experience-containers`, "Size and position") says: *"the scale components of the BillboardGui.Size property set the billboard's stud size in 3D space... [it] scales larger or smaller depending on its distance from the camera"*, and the class reference adds that the **offset** components behave like an ordinary screen-space `GuiObject` size. So `UDim2.fromOffset(2.6, 2.6)` is a 2.6-*pixel* canvas held at a fixed on-screen size — a pale smudge wider than it is tall by subpixel rounding, which is precisely what the screenshot showed — and only `UDim2.fromScale` means studs. The fix is one method call: `PICKUP_SPRITE_STUDS` is unchanged at **2.6**, and `PICKUP_SPRITE_STUDS`'s docblock now says it is meaningful *only* through `fromScale`, names the failure that taught us, and quotes the guide.

**The comment that argued for the wrong component is rewritten in place.** It read "**Offset is studs, not pixels.** A billboard's `Size` offset components are world studs, which is why this is `PICKUP_SPRITE_STUDS` and not a pixel count that would shrink with the camera distance." Every clause of that was backwards, so it now states the two-component rule, what the old line built, and which half of it was wrong.

**Two diagnostics, because "blank" and "too small to see" are indistinguishable from outside.** Neither changes behaviour; both are one line.

- On the first attach, `[PickupSprite] first sprite on <pad> size=<n> studs drawn=<w>x<h>px lift=<n> studs`. `drawn` is the `ImageLabel.AbsoluteSize` read a frame later, so it is the engine's answer rather than a restatement of the constant: a 2.6-pixel billboard reports `3x3px`, a correct one reports the same number in the hundreds depending on distance. One line per session, not per pad — the constants are shared, so the second pad cannot disagree.
- At boot, `ContentProvider.PreloadAsync` reports `[PickupSprite] image loaded <id>` or, on `Failure`/`TimedOut`, that the id did not resolve and which constant to check. An `ImageLabel` whose `Image` the engine cannot fetch draws **nothing at all**, which reads exactly like "the billboard is too small" — so the fetch status is now asked for once, at the only place it is observable. The likeliest cause of a `Failure` is an id that is not an image: a `Decal`'s asset id rather than its texture's, or a mesh/model id pasted into `PICKUP_SPRITE_ASSET_ID`. The pads collect and the sound fires either way.

**Audit.** Changed: `src/shared/tuning.ts` (one `fromOffset`-is-studs docblock replaced, constant value back to 2.6), `src/client/controllers/pickup-sprite-controller.ts` (the `Size` call, the wrong comment, `ContentProvider` import, `reportedFirstAttach`, `reportImageLoad`). Build exit 0, lint 0 problems, prettier clean, `\uXXXX` zero, `flamework.build` still **28 identifiers** (no new controller, so no regeneration). **`npm test` not run**, per the standing instruction. The spin, the throttle, the `Touched` caveat, the server body, `pickupDecision` and the sound are all untouched.

**Studio-only:** whether 2.6 studs now reads at the right size beside a 2-stud pad and a 1-stud ball; whether `135266450823195` resolves to an image (the new boot line answers this on the next playtest, and a blank sprite with `image loaded` printed means the id is an image this experience cannot use); whether the 1.7-stud lift still clears the ball that collects it now that the sprite is visible; and whether a `BillboardGui`'s roll really follows the camera's up closely enough to read as upright through the belt's banking.

## 146. The footprint ring is drawn from the collider, on the collider's floor, and the cylinder's face is not its `Top`

**Extends items 143/144/145 (the invisible pad and the visuals the client builds for it), 42 (`PICKUP_SIZE`, the collider's size), 80 (a `recycle` pad survives, so its ring does), 99 (a face decoration draws on a fully transparent part — extended here from `Decal`/`Texture` to `SurfaceGui`) and 15 (the cylinder's `X` axis).** Deliberately does **not** touch `onPickupTouched`, `pickupDecision`, `speedAfterPickup`, the pickup sound's throttle, the sprite's billboard, or the pad's collider.

**The problem was that a player could not see how close was close enough.** The pad is invisible (item 143) and the sprite floats 1.7 studs above it, so the sprite says *a pickup is here* and says nothing about the `Touched` volume on the floor. The ring is the second half of that sentence and it is drawn from the **pad's own `Size`, read at creation** — never from `PICKUP_SPRITE_STUDS`, which is the sprite's world scale and would drift apart from the collider the first time anyone retuned the picture.

**The ring is an annulus, not a filled disc.** `Frame` at scale `1,1`, `BackgroundTransparency = 1`, `UICorner` at `new UDim(1, 0)` (a full radius on a square frame is a circle), and all of the visible colour in one `UIStroke` that traces that circle. The disc lost on one fact: the ball that is about to collect the pad stands in the **middle** of the footprint, so a filled disc's most legible half is the half the ball covers. A boundary says "put your centre inside this" and survives being occupied — and the ring's diameter equals the ball's clearance, not its width.

**Cylinder geometry, and the trap in it.** `Enum.PartType.Cylinder` is *"a cylinder shape oriented along the **X** axis"*, so `Size.X` is the axis length and `Y`/`Z` are one diameter: the part is `(RING_THICKNESS_STUDS, diameter, diameter)`. `CFrame.Angles(0, 0, math.pi / 2)` stands that axis up, which puts the flat circular faces on world ±Y — the same turn `BallSpawnerService.attachBallMarkers` uses for the equator ring. **The consequence is that the upward face is not `Enum.NormalId.Top`.** `SurfaceGui.Face` is the part's *local* normal, and rotating local +X onto world +Y makes the sky-facing face the part's `Right`; the intuitive `Top` would draw the ring on the disc's vertical rim, edge-on to a camera looking down the belt, which is the same as not drawing it.

**`UIStroke.Thickness` is canvas pixels, not studs** — item 145's unit trap one property over, and the reason the brief's `2` was not used. A `SurfaceGui` rasterises at `PixelsPerStud x studs`, so the ring is a `400 x 400` canvas (`RING_PIXELS_PER_STUD = 200`) and the stroke is `6` of those pixels, i.e. `0.03` studs. Written as `2` it would have been `0.01` studs — a two-pixel line on a 400-pixel circle, present in Studio at 4x zoom and gone from the game camera.

**The ring floats `RING_LIFT_STUDS = 0.02` above the pad's bottom face, and that is a depth-buffer fix rather than a look.** `positionFor` puts the pad's bottom exactly on the surface a ball rests on — the invisible moving collider, itself `BELT_SURFACE_THICKNESS` thick — so a ring at that height is coplanar with the floor it describes and z-fights it. `SurfaceGui.ZOffset` was not used: it layers one `SurfaceGui` against another on the same face, which is a different question.

**The ring shows the footprint, and the ring is deliberately smaller than the volume.** The disc is inscribed in the pad's square cross-section (`min(Size.X, Size.Z)`), so every point inside the ring collects, while the square's four corners collect and sit outside the ring — the ring understates, which is the forgiving direction for a player aiming at it. The corollary is worth writing down because it will be reported as a bug: **a ball's *edge* touching the rim is not a collection.** A 1-stud ball whose rim just reaches a 2-stud ring has its centre `1.5` studs from the pad's centre, i.e. outside a collider whose half-width is `1`. Collection is the ball's *centre* entering the box.

**The ring is `Playing`-only because the pad is, and no phase guard was added for it.** `PickupService` spawns pads only in `Playing` and destroys them on every other phase; the ring is a child of the pad. A guard would be a second, hand-maintained copy of a rule the parent already implements.

**One coupling was removed while building it: the ring is drawn even when no sprite image resolves.** The sprite depends on `this.imageUri`; the ring depends on the pad's `Size` and nothing else. `attach` now builds the ring first and unconditionally, `buildSprite` returns `undefined` on a session with no image, and `SpriteRecord.label` is optional — so a missing or unloadable asset costs the picture and not the footprint, which is the visual that was built to be legible without a texture in the first place.

**Two lines, and why the brief's single boot line could not carry both facts.** At boot there is no pad, so a boot line cannot print a pad's real `Size`; it prints the ring's *look* instead — `colour`, `transparency`, `stroke` (in px), `pixels`/stud, `thickness`, `lift` — so a "the ring looks wrong" report can quote a value rather than describe a colour. The pad's measured numbers go on the **existing** first-attach line (item 145's), which now reads `sprite=… drawn=… lift=… pad=<x>x<y>x<z> ring=<diameter> studs`. No new per-pad line.

**Audit.** Changed: `src/client/controllers/pickup-sprite-controller.ts` (class docblock rewritten for two visuals, `buildFootprint`, `buildSprite` split out of `attach`, optional `record.label`, ring constants in the boot line, `FootprintInfo`), `src/shared/tuning.ts` (`RING_COLOR`, `RING_TRANSPARENCY`, `RING_STROKE_THICKNESS`, `RING_PIXELS_PER_STUD`, `RING_THICKNESS_STUDS`, `RING_LIFT_STUDS`), `README.md` (one line). Build exit 0, lint 0 problems, prettier clean, `\uXXXX` zero, `flamework.build` unchanged at **28 identifiers** (no new controller). **`npm test` not run**, per the standing instruction.

**Placeholders:** `RING_TRANSPARENCY` (0.5), `RING_STROKE_THICKNESS` (6, canvas px), `RING_PIXELS_PER_STUD` (200), `RING_THICKNESS_STUDS` (0.05), `RING_LIFT_STUDS` (0.02). `RING_COLOR` is the user's hex and is **not** a placeholder.

**Studio-only:** whether `0.5` on `#00BFFF` reads as "transparent sky blue" or as "electric cyan" on a dark belt (the docblock points at `RING_TRANSPARENCY`, not at the colour, if it is the latter); whether a 6-pixel annulus is legible at the game camera's pitch; whether `UIStroke` traces the `UICorner` circle on a fully transparent `Frame` as expected; whether `SurfaceGui` draws on a `Transparency = 1` part — item 99 established it for `Decal`/`Texture` and this assumes the same for a face gui, unverified; and whether the ring and the ball overlap in a way that hides the ball.

## 147. The footprint is a filled disc at `0.6` — item 146's annulus, reversed, with its argument kept as the record of why
