**Extends items 146 (the ring round this one reverses) and 99 (a face decoration draws on a fully transparent part).** This is a deliberate reversal, not a refinement: item 146 chose an annulus and argued for it; the user has decided the opposite, so the argument is **rewritten in place** rather than deleted, and this item exists so the two rounds do not read as a disagreement.

**What changed, exactly.**

- `Frame.BackgroundColor3 = RING_COLOR` and `Frame.BackgroundTransparency = RING_TRANSPARENCY` — the fill is the visual.
- `UICorner` at `new UDim(1, 0)` stays; it is now what turns the drawn rectangle into a disc rather than what a stroke traced. (`new UDim(1, 0)`, not `UDim.new`: `@rbxts/types` declares `type UDimConstructor = new (scale?, offset?) => UDim` at `include/roblox.d.ts:2540`, so `.new` does not compile — the same finding item 146 hit as a build error.)
- `UIStroke` **deleted**. A stroke in the same colour at the same transparency as its own fill is not an edge, it is the fill drawn a second time along the rim: a seam at some distances, nothing at others. An edge earns its place when it says something the fill cannot, and the fill already says where the boundary is.
- `RING_STROKE_THICKNESS` **deleted from `tuning.ts`**, not left at `0` — a constant with no reader is the thing item 144 removed the pad's `Color` for. Its docblock (the canvas-pixel unit trap) is gone with it; that trap is recorded in item 146 and in `RING_PIXELS_PER_STUD`'s new paragraph.
- `RING_TRANSPARENCY` `0.5` → `0.6`. **It keeps `Placeholder.`**, because a fill is far more sensitive to the number than a 6-pixel outline was: the same value reads heavier on a light asset than a dark one and heavier from a low pitch than from above, so `0.6` is the user's starting point rather than a designed final.
- `RING_PIXELS_PER_STUD` stays `200`, with a **different** justification: with an outline, the density and the stroke width were coupled (a 2-pixel line on a 100-pixel canvas is a quarter of the ring). With a fill, density only decides how smooth the edge against the belt is, and 400 pixels across a 2-stud disc is already finer than a stud by an order of magnitude — there is nothing left to buy.

**The annulus argument, kept and answered.** Item 146 wrote: "the ball that is about to collect the pad stands in the middle of the footprint, so a filled disc's most legible half is the half the ball covers. A boundary says 'put your centre inside this' and survives being occupied." **That is still true** — a ball at the centre does hide the middle of a disc. It lost because the two shapes say different things: a boundary says *cross this line*, and a pickup actually offers an *area* you have to get the ball's centre into. A fill reads as that area from further away than a thin line does, and the cost is paid only by the pad that is about to be collected anyway. The comment in `buildFootprint` now states both halves, names item 147, and points at the reversal.

**The inscribed-circle geometry is unchanged, and the corners are still the caveat.** Diameter is `min(pad.Size.X, pad.Size.Z) = 2` on the `2 x 1 x 2` collider, so the four corners of the square collect and sit outside the disc. That was true of the annulus too — it is a property of drawing a circle on a square, not of the fill — and the docblock says so rather than letting a future round read it as a new understatement.

**Logging.** The boot ring line is now
`[PickupSprite] ring shape=disc colour=<r>,<g>,<b> transparency=<n> pixels=<n>/stud thickness=<n> lift=<n>`.
`stroke=` is gone with its constant; `shape=disc` is new so the line cannot be read against item 146's log and mistaken for the same shape. **`thickness=` stays and is not the stroke** — it prints `RING_THICKNESS_STUDS`, the slab's own axis length, which the disc still has because a `SurfaceGui` needs a face. The brief asked for both fields to go; one of them was never the stroke. The channels are also wrapped in `math.round`: `Color3.fromRGB` stores `n / 255`, so `191 / 255 * 255` prints as `190.99999999999997` in the one line whose job is to be comparable to a hex.

**Unchanged, deliberately:** the pad and `PICKUP_SIZE`; the sprite's billboard and `PICKUP_SPRITE_STUDS`; the ordering that builds the footprint before the image guard (item 146 — a missing asset costs the picture, not the disc); the `Right` face, the lift, the inscribed diameter, `LightInfluence = 0`, `AlwaysOnTop = false`, and the ring being `Playing`-only because the pad is.

**Audit.** Changed: `src/client/controllers/pickup-sprite-controller.ts` (the `Frame` block and its docblock, `UIStroke` block deleted, the "no stroke" note, boot line, `RING_STROKE_THICKNESS` import removed, class docblock now says "filled disc"), `src/shared/tuning.ts` (`RING_TRANSPARENCY` to `0.6` and rewritten, `RING_STROKE_THICKNESS` deleted, `RING_COLOR`'s and `RING_PIXELS_PER_STUD`'s docblocks updated), `README.md` (one clause). Build exit 0, lint 0 problems, prettier clean, `\uXXXX` zero, `RING_STROKE_THICKNESS` grep zero, `flamework.build` unchanged at **28 identifiers**. **`npm test` not run.**

**Placeholders:** `RING_TRANSPARENCY` (0.6 — kept, see above), `RING_PIXELS_PER_STUD` (200), `RING_THICKNESS_STUDS` (0.05), `RING_LIFT_STUDS` (0.02). `RING_COLOR` is the user's hex and is **not** a placeholder.

**Studio-only:** whether `0.6` on `#00BFFF` reads as a transparent zone rather than a solid plate against the belt's texture; whether the filled disc's **edge** is legible at all — an annulus has a drawn edge, a fill has only the boundary between `RING_COLOR` at `0.6` and whatever is behind it, and if that is not enough the answer is a second, darker filled frame (a rim) rather than bringing the stroke back; whether a `UICorner`ed `Frame` is a clean circle at `200` px/stud or shows its tessellation; whether the disc at the ball's centre hides the ball at the camera's pitch; and — carried over from item 146 and still unverified — whether a `SurfaceGui` draws on a `Transparency = 1` part at all, which this round did not re-test and cannot tell apart from the fill itself being wrong.

## 148. A decoy twin is destroyed with its parent — the rule in `forgetDecoy`, the timing on the parent's own death signal

**Extends items 77/79 (the twin and its owner-only outline) and 129 (the twin's identity on the leaderboard).** Does not touch the winner rule, `spawnDecoy`'s body construction, `decoyFor`, `decoy-outline-controller`, or anything from 143–147.

**What was actually wrong — the third of the brief's three possibilities.** Both death paths *do* clear the link, and `forgetDecoy` *did not* destroy the twin: it was **deliberate**. Item 79's docblock said "a parent's death leaves an orphaned twin on the belt — the twin is not a child of the parent, deliberately, because `Destroy()` on the parent must not silently remove a body the round may still be counting", and item 129 then *depended* on the orphan: the twin's identity snapshot existed so a leftover twin would not publish as `Decoy B7`. So the twin outliving its parent was a design, not an omission — and the user has now decided it is wrong, because a body with nobody in it keeps racing after the player it belongs to has been eliminated.

**The call sites, named.** `forgetDecoy` has exactly three callers: `destroyBall` (the `KillY` and live-ball-cap path — synchronous, before the body's own `Destroy()`), `pruneDestroyedBalls` (any body that left the world by another route, which is how a `left-belt` elimination is noticed, since `RoundService.settleEliminations` destroys the body itself), and — new this round — the parent's own `Destroying` signal.

**Two mechanisms, and the split is deliberate.** `forgetDecoy` owns the *rule* ("a twin dies with its parent"), so every caller that drops a link drops the body too, including callers that do not exist yet. The parent's `Destroying` signal in `spawnDecoy` owns the *timing*: the cleanup pass runs every `CLEANUP_INTERVAL_SECONDS` (0.5 s), so a `left-belt` elimination would otherwise leave a fake ball standing on the belt for up to half a second — precisely the leftover-body artifact this round exists to remove. `Destroying` fires inside the `Destroy()` call, whichever path made it, so the twin is gone in the same frame as the parent. Both call the same function; the second finds no entry and does nothing.

**The double-destroy guard is the map, and a `Parent` test beside it.** `decoysByParent.get(ball)` is read *before* the delete, because that value is the only reference to the twin on the parent's side; the delete is also what makes a repeat call a no-op. The destroy is then gated on `twin !== undefined && twin !== ball && twin.Parent !== undefined`, so a twin that is the body being forgotten, or one already destroyed by its own cull or a teardown, is skipped rather than re-destroyed.

**The added destroy path cannot reach the round's accounting — verified, not assumed.** `RoundService.trackBall` is called only for bodies returned by `spawnInLane`/`spawnForRound`, i.e. **parents**; twins live in the *spawner's* `liveBalls` and never in the round's. So the twin's `Destroying` reaches `handleExternalDestruction`, which returns on its first line (`!this.liveBalls.has(ball)`). Belt and braces, the rest of that method would also have been silent for an ownerless body: `recordElimination(undefined)` skips by design, `splashTargetUserId(undefined, "culled")` returns `undefined` (its own spec'd rule), and `playEliminationSound` returns on `owner === undefined`. No splash, no payout, no second leaderboard event, no `evaluateAfterLoss`.

**A twin that dies first leaves nothing behind.** Its own death reaches `forgetDecoy(twin)`, whose reverse scan deletes the parent's entry, so `decoyFor(parent)` answers `undefined` from then on (it already had a `Parent === undefined` guard as a second line of defence) and a later `forgetDecoy(parent)` finds no twin to destroy.

**Three docblocks argued for the old behaviour and are rewritten in place, not deleted:** `forgetDecoy`'s (the orphan paragraph now says the rule reversed, and keeps the "not a child of the parent" fact while flipping its conclusion), `decoyIdentities`' ("keeping the entry through the parent's death is the whole point" — that case is now impossible, so the map is kept for the surviving reason: one map read instead of a reverse scan for a body that has no owner attributes of its own), and `decoysByParent`'s (the link is a record of a *pair* and is meaningless once either half dies; the identity is a fact about a body still on the belt).

**One diagnostic, and it is temporary.** `[Decoy] twin <name> destroyed with parent <name>`, marked `TEMPORARY INSTRUMENTATION` in place: the twin's disappearance is otherwise unobservable — the parent has its `[Round] eliminated` line and the twin has nothing, so a round that failed to take it would look exactly like one that did. At most one line per lane per round.

**No spec added, and the reason.** `forgetDecoy` is not pure in the sense `round-outcome.ts` or `motion-blur.ts` are: its whole job is instance identity in a `Map<BasePart, BasePart>`, and the only way to assert it is to build real `BasePart`s. A spec that faked them would assert the fake. With `npm test` off the table this round there is also no way to find out whether such a spec even runs, and an unverified spec is worse than a stated Studio-only check.

**Audit.** Changed: `src/server/services/ball-spawner-service.ts` only (the twin capture and destroy in `forgetDecoy`, the `Destroying` hook in `spawnDecoy`, three docblocks). Build exit 0, lint 0 problems, prettier clean, `\uXXXX` zero, `flamework.build` unchanged at **28 identifiers**. **`npm test` not run.**

**Placeholders:** none invented this round.

**Studio-only:** whether the twin now goes with the parent on both paths (the one temporary line says whether the code took it; only a playtest says whether a player ever sees the orphan), whether anything still names a twin on the leaderboard after its parent is out (it should not be listed at all now), and whether destroying the twin mid-tick ever races a `settleEliminations` pass into touching a body it had already seen — the cleanup pass and the round tick are independent loops, and only a live round exercises that overlap.

## 149. The picker gives up twelve seconds and a 3-2-1-Start! countdown takes the last two

**Extends items 34/37/38 (the phase machine and its four values), 36/131 (bodies spawn at `Waiting` entry, so `Waiting` is already a frozen scene), 69/70 (the picker and its server-clock countdown), 73 (the splash idiom this animation follows) and 116 (`outlineText`).** Does **not** add a phase, a `RoundState` value, or a single line of `Playing` freeze code; does not touch `motionBlur`, `RoundSong`, pickups, the winner rule, the phase banner, `spawnRoundCompetitors`, `enterPlaying`'s transition logic, or the picker's appearance.

**The countdown lives in `Waiting` because `Waiting` is already frozen.** `enterWaiting` sets the belt to 0 and `setRoundActive(false)`, and the bodies arrived at `Waiting` entry (`startWaitingRound` → `spawnRoundCompetitors`, called before `enterWaiting` from both entry paths). So there is nothing to hold back: **no freeze code was added, and none is needed**. `RoundState` stays `Waiting` throughout, which is what the banner shows.

**`PICKER_WINDOW_SECONDS = 12`, and the window now closes on its own timer.** This is the part of the brief that was incomplete: the pick window used to close at `enterPlaying`, i.e. *because* the phase ended, so shortening its deadline alone would have left the panel up and the server accepting picks for the last three seconds. The window now ends at `pickerDeadline`, server-side via `armPickWindowClose` (guarded on the deadline token and the phase) and client-side by `picker-controller.tickCountdown` hiding the panel when the countdown reaches zero. `enterPlaying` keeps its own `closeOffers` call as the backstop for a path that never opened offers.

**`ReplicatedStorage.PlayingDeadline`** — a `NumberValue`, the third of the `RoundState`/`WinnerName` family, seeded `0` at startup, written in `enterWaiting`, cleared at `Playing` entry and at `Intermission` entry, and **set to `0` by a re-armed `Waiting`** so a lobby with no competitors does not put a 3-2-1 in front of a state that will fail the same guard again fifteen seconds later. One writer (`publishPlayingDeadline`), as with the other two.

**The bug the round found on the way, and the reason the pick window's arithmetic moved.** `openOffers` read `pendingTimerHold` — but it runs from `startWaitingRound`, *before* `transitionAround` sets that hold for the wipe. So the picker's deadline was measured from the moment the offers were **rolled**, which on an automatic round is behind the transition cover, while the phase ends `cover + hold + open` later. Today that showed as the panel sitting at `0` for ~3.5 s; with a 12 s window it would have been ~4 s of nothing between the panel closing and the countdown starting, on real rounds only, with debug rounds looking correct. **The fix is one arithmetic, moved to the one place that knows it:** `enterWaiting` consumes the hold, computes `endsAt = now + WAITING_SECONDS + hold`, publishes it, and derives `pickerDeadline = endsAt - (WAITING_SECONDS - PICKER_WINDOW_SECONDS)`. The *roll* stays in `openOffers` (the body needs its pick before it is spawned, item 36); the *send* moved to `announceOffers`, called from `enterWaiting`, because every offer message carries that deadline. `scheduleWaitingTimeout` no longer reads the hold — it is handed the delay. Net effect: the panel closes 0.9 s before the `3` appears, on a wiped round exactly as on a `2`-press round.

**`shared/ui/countdown.ts` — the timeline as data.** `countdownSteps(timing)` builds a contiguous partition of the sequence (`in`/`out` per caption, then `hold`/`fade` for `Start!`), `countdownDuration(steps)` folds the total, and `countdownStepIndex(steps, elapsed)` answers "which step is it now". The controller is then a per-frame lookup against `deadline - COUNTDOWN_SECONDS`, never a chain of `task.delay`s — a chain would start from the client's arrival, drift by every hitch, and give a late joiner nothing. **The arithmetic was executed, not asserted:** the module was compiled standalone with `tsc` and run under `node` (a scratch shim for roblox-ts's `Array.size`, deleted afterwards), which printed a 2.1000 s total, nine steps contiguous to the last digit, and the exact boundary behaviour at 0.19/0.2, 0.35, 0.55, 0.70, 0.90, 1.05, 1.25, 1.849/1.85 and 2.09/2.10.

**The animation, verbatim from the brief:** outgoing scale `1 → 1.85` with transparency `0 → 1` over 0.15 s, incoming `6 → 1` with `1 → 0` over 0.2 s, `Quad`/`Out` throughout, no overlap (the steps are contiguous), `Start!` held 0.6 s then faded over 0.25 s with **no** zoom. Five `Placeholder.` timings in `countdown-controller.ts`, and the tweens of a step are cancelled when the next one starts, because a client that hitched can arrive mid-tween and two tweens on one property fight.

**Typography and geometry.** `GothamBlack` (the poster weight `payout-controller`, `reward-toast-controller` and the leaderboard title use) rather than the game's `GothamMedium`; a **fixed** 720×220 box with `TextSize = 144` rather than `AutomaticSize` or `TextScaled`, because both of those interact with the `UIScale` that is doing the zoom — `TextScaled` re-typesets at every step and `AutomaticSize` recomputes from content that the scale is also multiplying. Centred alignment keeps `3`, `2` and `Start!` on one centre line. The `UIScale` sits on the label and the label is anchored at the screen centre, so the sweep grows symmetrically: `UIScale.Scale` is documented as "the multiplier to apply to the parent UI element's **size**", which is why the anchor point rather than the text position does the centring.

**`outlineText` now returns its `UIStroke`.** A stroke's transparency is its own property (the finding `payout-controller` records for text outlines), so anything that fades a label has to fade the outline separately — and it cannot do that through a function that returns nothing without building a second stroke, which is the one thing `outlineText` exists to prevent. Callers that only want the outline ignore the return. The countdown then tunes two of its numbers for a poster (`shadow` colour, 4 px) and leaves the creation in one place.

**Logs.** `[Countdown] mounted layer=splash font=GothamBlack duration=2.1s captions=9` · `start playingDeadline=<t> duration=2.1s startsIn=<n>s` (`startsIn` is negative for a client that joined mid-sequence, which is the fact the deadline alone cannot show) · `caption=<3|2|1|Start!> remaining=<n>s` · `done` · `skipped (deadline past by <n>s)`. Plus `[Picker] window closed after 12s` (server) and `[Picker] closed deadline=<t>` (client).

**Audit.** New: `src/client/controllers/countdown-controller.ts`, `src/shared/ui/countdown.ts`. Changed: `src/shared/remotes.ts` (`PLAYING_DEADLINE_VALUE_NAME`), `src/shared/tuning.ts` (`PICKER_WINDOW_SECONDS`), `src/shared/ui/text.ts` (`outlineText` returns the stroke), `src/server/services/round-service.ts` (the deadline value and its writer, `enterWaiting` as the one place the phase end is computed, `scheduleWaitingTimeout(generation, delay)`, `openOffers`/`announceOffers`/`armPickWindowClose`, the two clears), `src/client/controllers/picker-controller.ts` (hide at the deadline), `README.md` (phase line, picker bullet, countdown bullet, walkthrough step 3, controller count). Build exit 0, lint 0 problems, prettier clean, `\uXXXX` zero, `flamework.build` **regenerated to 29 identifiers** with `CountdownController` present. **`npm test` not run.** One build error worth recording: `let end` is a reserved Luau identifier and `roblox-ts` rejects it, so the fold in `countdownDuration` uses `latest`.

**Placeholders:** `PICKER_WINDOW_SECONDS` (12), `CAPTION_OUT_SECONDS` (0.15), `CAPTION_IN_SECONDS` (0.2), `START_HOLD_SECONDS` (0.6), `START_FADE_SECONDS` (0.25), `SCALE_SWEPT` (1.85), `SCALE_INCOMING` (6), `TEXT_SIZE` (144), `BOX_WIDTH`/`BOX_HEIGHT` (720/220), `OUTLINE_THICKNESS` (4), `REPLICATED_WAIT_SECONDS` (10). `COUNTDOWN_FONT` is a choice, not a tuned number.

**Studio-only:** whether `GothamBlack` at 144 px reads over the belt through the outline; whether 0.15/0.2 s `Quad`/`Out` reads as "rushing toward the camera" rather than as a slideshow; whether the 0.9 s gap feels like a breath or like a stall (and whether it should absorb a longer `Start!` hold instead); whether the `UIScale` at 6× on first frame overdraws anything visible; whether a late joiner sees a coherent mid-sequence caption; and whether the countdown and the phase banner collide visually in the top third of the screen (the banner is the HUD layer, the countdown the splash layer, so the countdown draws over it).

## 150. Bots for a solo Studio round, and `/dev` that will not change a real player's balance by reflex

**Extends items 36/38 (spawn-then-enter and the `Playing → Playing` restart), 65/67 (`/dev`, its parser and its spec), 72 (one competitor is the winner — the bug both halves are about), 73 (the key map), 131 (the bots this round relocates), 135 (`isStudioSession`) and 149 (the `Waiting` countdown, which now plays over bots that were already there).** Does not touch the winner rule, the countdown, `motionBlur`, `RoundSong`, `ADMIN_USER_IDS`, any admin subcommand's body, `isStudioSession()` itself, or the non-admin refusal string.

**Two safety defaults, both seeded from one environment read.** Studio is where the conveniences belong and Live is where a slip is expensive: a Studio round gets bots automatically so a solo playtest is a race, and a live server arrives with the dangerous `/dev` verbs **disarmed**. Neither is a security control — `ADMIN_USER_IDS` is the access control and the token is one keystroke of friction — and both docblocks say so.

**`spawnBots(reason)` is `debugSpawnCompetitors` minus the gate.** Item 87's `playEliminationSound` split, reused: the rule (`Playing` or `Waiting`) stays in `debugSpawnCompetitors`, and the four callers that already know their phase call `spawnBots` directly. **The body is byte-identical** — same `getBoundSpawnerCount()`, same synthetic `Debug#N` owners, same tracking, same log line as key `4` has always printed: `[Round] debug spawn (<reason>): <n> competitors (<first>..<last>) balls=<ids>, live=<n>`. The reason text now names the path (`studio-auto`, `debug key 3`, `debug key 3 restart`, `auto-bots for debug key 2`), which is the one change and it is a log field item 131 already had.

**The automatic population lives in `startWaitingRound`, not in `forceWaiting`.** That is the one place `Waiting` begins, so both keys and the `Intermission` timer are covered by one call, in every round rather than only the one key `2` starts — item 131's call sat only on the key. `spawnStudioBots()` returns `0` unless the session is Studio **and** `Players.GetPlayers().size() === 1`, and `startWaitingRound` only calls it when `spawnRoundCompetitors` produced at least one player body: bots in a lobby that is about to re-arm `Intermission` would be synthetic bodies on an idle belt, and because a bot carries an `OwnerUserId` it would satisfy `enterPlaying`'s guard and start a race with nobody in it. The returned count includes the bots so `enterWaiting`'s `competitors=` still matches the world.

**Key `2` keeps item 131's behaviour where it is not already covered.** `forceWaiting` now calls `IS_STUDIO ? 0 : spawnBots("auto-bots for debug key 2")` — in Studio the automatic call has already done it, and on Live a human pressed a debug verb on purpose, so it still populates. Item 131's docblock argued for an unconditional call and is rewritten in place rather than deleted: the reasoning that was right (a Studio session needs company) is now served one function up.

**Key `3` spawns bots in both of its bodies.** `forcePlaying` has two: the `Playing → Playing` restart branch and the fresh-entry tail. Both call `spawnBots` **after** their `spawned === 0` guard and **before** `enterPlaying`, so an empty belt still stays empty and `Playing` entry's `competitors=` counts them. Unconditional rather than Studio-gated, on the same argument as key `2` on Live.

**`/dev` grew an arming gate, and the parser had to grow with it.** `parseDevCommand` had **no** `arm` case: `/dev arm …` fell into `unknown subcommand`, so there was no route from the chat line to an arming call at all. `DevCommand` therefore gained `{kind: "arm"; token}` and `{kind: "disarm"}` and the parser two branches — `arm` accepts zero or one token (a bare `/dev arm` yields `token = ""`, which fails the *token comparison* rather than the parse, so every wrong attempt reads the same), `disarm` accepts none. This is the one place the brief was self-contradictory: it required `arm` to reach the handler *and* forbade changing the parser's shape. The shape changed by two variants; no existing variant, field or refusal moved.

**`admin.ts` holds the state, the rule, and three wrappers.** `DEV_ARM_TOKEN = "arm-dev"` (**Placeholder.**, not a secret — a leaked token is not a breach because the admin list is the access control). `armDev(state, token)` and `disarmDev(state)` are **pure**: state in, state out, which is what makes all five branches assertable in Jest Lua. `armSessionDev(player, token)`, `disarmSessionDev()` and `disarmSessionDevFor(userId)` are the only code that reads or writes `devArmed` / `armedByUserId` / `armedByDisplayName`; the handler names none of them. The token is compared **before** the armed test, so a wrong token always reports `bad-token` and never leaks whether the door is open.

**The handler is `authorise → parse → arm | disarm | gate → resolve → dispatch`,** and the gate sits exactly there. `/dev arm <bad>` and every unarmed subcommand both refuse through **one helper**, `refuseUnrecognised`, which is also the non-admin refusal — so the two strings cannot drift, and the line an unarmed admin sees says "is not an admin" about them. That is deliberate and stated: a wrong token must be indistinguishable from a wrong account in the log. The unarmed path adds a second line, `[Admin] /dev <sub> refused (not armed) by <name>`, so the reason is still readable to the one person who can act on it.

**Disarm on armer-leave**, connected in `EconomyService.onStart` to `Players.PlayerRemoving` → `disarmSessionDevFor(player.UserId)`, which returns `not-the-armer` (and does nothing) unless the departing player is the one who armed it, and logs `[Admin] /dev DISARMED (armer left) <name>/<displayName>`. A *rejoining* admin needs no re-arm: the flag is server-session state, so it closed when they left and only `/dev arm` opens it again. Another admin leaving does not close somebody else's session.

**One environment read per file.** `round-service.ts` holds `const IS_STUDIO = isStudioSession()` at module scope and three call sites read it; `admin.ts` holds `const IS_STUDIO = isStudioSession()` and both its seed (`let devArmed = IS_STUDIO`) and the boot line's `reason=` read that one constant. Two reads per boot, one per file. A `RunService.IsStudio()` per call site would be five reads that are each individually correct and collectively able to disagree.

**Boot line:** `[Admin] /dev registered; authed=server-only armed=<true|false> reason=<studio|live>` — on a live server the first evidence that a playtest's arming did not carry over.

**Spec.** `admin.spec.ts` gains eleven cases across three blocks, all against the pure functions with literal state: `armDev` (arms; wrong token leaves state *identical by reference*; wrong token on an armed session still says `bad-token`; `already-armed`; the empty token a bare `/dev arm` produces) and `disarmDev` (clears `by*`; no-ops on a disarmed state), plus the parser's two new subcommands and their arities. **`isDevArmed`, the module seed and the three wrappers are Studio-only** and are not asserted: they depend on the environment the suite runs in and on a module singleton the rest of the file would then see mutated.

**Audit.** Changed: `src/server/admin.ts` (import, token, state, two pure rules, three wrappers, two parser branches, one accessor), `src/server/services/economy-service.ts` (import, boot line, `refuseUnrecognised`, the gate and the two bypasses, `disarmIfArmerLeft`, one `PlayerRemoving` connection), `src/server/services/round-service.ts` (`IS_STUDIO`, `spawnBots` extracted, `spawnStudioBots`, three call sites, item 131's docblock rewritten), `src/server/test/admin.spec.ts` (eleven cases), `README.md` (keys `2`/`3`, the `/dev` bullet, a bots bullet). Build exit 0, lint 0 problems, prettier clean, `\uXXXX` zero, `DEV_ARM_TOKEN` grep finds it only in `admin.ts`, `flamework.build` unchanged at **29 identifiers**. **`npm test` not run.**

**Placeholders:** `DEV_ARM_TOKEN` (`"arm-dev"`). `ADMIN_COIN_CAP` and `ADMIN_USER_IDS` remain non-placeholders, per item 65.

**Studio-only:** whether bots are visible during the 3-2-1 countdown (they spawn at `Waiting` entry, so they should be standing on the belt in the frozen scene); whether a solo Studio round reliably has ≥2 competitors at `Playing` entry when the scene has a single bound spawner; whether `/dev arm` reaches `Triggered` at all under the engine's chat filtering (the same unknown item 65 carried, now on the path that opens a door); whether `PlayerRemoving` fires early enough that the `Player` reference is still readable in the handler; and whether `MaxLiveBalls` survives auto-Studio plus key `3` plus key `4` stacked in one session.

## 151. The sway added its rate to the ball's existing sideways velocity instead of setting it — so the field was one undamped oscillator, not a crowd

**Reported: "why these balls all swaying the same direction, at the same time? or is it freak chance?"** Not chance. The phases *are* drawn independently (`math.random() * SWAY_PHASE_JITTER`, `SWAY_PHASE_JITTER = math.pi`), so the design was already the crowd. **The ball's drawn phase was not what the motion was following.**

**The defect is one term, and the docblock had already stated the rule it broke.** The sway branch wrote

```ts
ball.AssemblyLinearVelocity = velocity.sub(right.mul(along)).add(right.mul(-relative)).add(lateral);
```

`velocity` is the **current** assembly velocity, which already contains last tick's lateral component. `sub(right.mul(along))` removes only the along-belt part, so the lateral part was **kept** and this tick's `lateralRate` was **added to it**. Item 107's own comment above that branch says the sway "rewrites" the lateral component and that "a ball knocked sideways has its sideways motion overwritten on the next tick rather than carried" — the code carried it.

**Why that makes the field move together, in arithmetic.** Writing the lateral velocity *sets* the position error's law to `e' = -e / T`, which decays in `T` and leaves `z(t) = A · sin(omega·t + phase)`. *Adding* to it makes the error obey `e'' = -e / T` — a harmonic oscillator whose poles sit **on** the unit circle, so it has no damping at all. Its period is the oscillator's (`2·pi·sqrt(T)` = 7.7 s analytically) rather than the wave's (10 s), and because nothing decays, the **startup transient never dies**: the amplitude and phase of each ball's motion are set by the transient, not by its drawn phase. Collisions then pump the same oscillator, which is one shared excitation across the whole field. `[Powers] hit` fires every few seconds in the log that prompted this, so the pump is constant.

**Verified by simulating the loop, not by reasoning about it.** Both variants were run in `node` at the real constants (`A = 2`, `omega = 2·pi·0.1`, `T = 1.5`, `dt = 1/60`) from rest, for three drawn phases:

| variant | amplitude | period | dependence on phase |
|---|---|---|---|
| `add` (the bug) | 3.8–5.5 studs | 1.1–3.1 s | amplitude and period both change with the drawn phase |
| `set` (the fix) | 2.00–2.01 studs | 10.00 s | none — only the *offset* changes, as a sine should |

The simulated amplitude for `add` also explains the log: the sampled ball's `localZ` runs to ±2.9 against `SWAY_AMPLITUDE = 2`, which the buggy model predicts and the correct one cannot produce. (In game the belt walls and the other balls clip that, so the numbers on screen are the clipped version of the same overshoot.)

**The fix:** subtract the carried lateral component before adding the new rate —

```ts
const carriedLateral = velocity.Dot(across);
ball.AssemblyLinearVelocity = velocity
    .sub(right.mul(along))
    .sub(across.mul(carriedLateral))
    .add(right.mul(-relative))
    .add(lateral);
```

`across` is horizontal, so the vertical component still belongs to gravity; the along-belt component is removed separately, as before. Item 107's paragraph that claimed the overwrite now also records that the claim is one the write has to earn.

**A diagnostic, because the log could not answer the question it was asked.** Only one ball is ever sampled (`sampleBall`), so no amount of `[Ball:1] sample` lines can say whether the *field* is in phase. The existing `[Spawner] round start:` line now carries every live ball's drawn phase:

`[Spawner] round start: 4 ball(s) at BALL_SPEED=… sway=2.975,0.412,1.884,3.07 (0..3.141592653589793)`

Once per round, four numbers. Independent draws that happen to cluster **are** chance and the knob is `SWAY_PHASE_JITTER`; identical values would be a defect in the draw.

**Audit.** Changed: `src/server/services/ball-spawner-service.ts` only (the lateral write, two docblock paragraphs, the round-start line). Build exit 0, lint 0 problems, prettier clean, `\uXXXX` zero, `flamework.build` unchanged at **29 identifiers**. **`npm test` not run.**

**Placeholders:** none invented; `SWAY_AMPLITUDE`, `SWAY_FREQUENCY_HZ`, `SWAY_PHASE_JITTER` and `SWAY_TRACK_SECONDS` are unchanged and still the four knobs.

**Studio-only:** whether the field now reads as a crowd (phases up to `pi` apart, each ball tracing its own 10 s sine at ±2 studs); whether the corrected sway is too gentle at `SWAY_AMPLITUDE = 2` now that it is no longer amplified by resonance — the constant was last tuned **against** the buggy motion, so it is the first thing to raise if the sway now looks timid; and whether wiping the carried lateral velocity each tick makes ball-to-ball collisions feel less deflecting (the docblock argues that is the intended model, but it is a feel, not a proof).

## 152. The countdown was fast because a caption had no readable frame — not because it started late

**Reported: "the countdown feels too fast."** Three candidates were offered in order. **Only the second and third were real; the first cannot be a cause of speed at all.**

**1. The alignment — declined, and it could not have worked.** The controller *can* reach the picker's close time: it is `playingDeadline - (WAITING_SECONDS - PICKER_WINDOW_SECONDS)`, and both constants are in `shared/tuning.ts`, so anchoring the sequence to the panel instead of to the phase was available. Two reasons it was not taken. First, **moving a fixed-length sequence changes when it happens, not how fast it is** — the tweens are identical wherever they sit, so the 0.9 s would simply relocate to the other end. Second, ending on `playingDeadline` is what makes `Start!` land *on* the start; ending at the picker's close replaces the cue with three quarters of a second of silent frozen belt, which reads as the countdown finishing before the race does. The sequence keeps the phase as its end and the *room* for it comes out of the pick window instead — see 3.

**2. The incoming scale — this was the actual defect, and it was worse than "off-screen".** `SCALE_INCOMING = 6` on a `BOX_HEIGHT = 220` label means the drawn box is **1320 px tall on a 1080 px viewport**. It is centred, so the caption is not *gone* — it is the middle of a letter filling more than the screen. A whole glyph only appears in the tail of the inbound tween, so the 0.2 s was mostly spent showing something unreadable and the number arrived as a flash. `2.7` keeps the "arriving from closer to camera" read (nearly three times resting size) while leaving a whole, legible number for the entire tween.

**3. The durations — raised, because 2.1 s was not the reference either.** `CAPTION_IN_SECONDS` 0.2 → **0.4**, `CAPTION_OUT_SECONDS` 0.15 → **0.2**, same 2:1 ratio so only the tempo moves, not the proportions. `START_HOLD_SECONDS` (0.6) and `START_FADE_SECONDS` (0.25) are untouched, as instructed.

**New total: 2.1 s → 3.05 s** — `3 × (0.4 + 0.2)` for the three digits, plus `0.4 + 0.6 + 0.25` for `Start!`. Computed from the same table the controller uses (`countdownDuration`), and checked by running the formula outside the engine before touching a constant.

**A caption now has a dwell it did not have.** At 0.2/0.15 the inbound tween ended exactly where the outbound began, so each digit was fully legible for **one frame**. The pair also now leaves roughly a tenth of a second on screen where the number is at rest; the honest reading of the complaint is that the sequence had no moment to read, and that is what both numbers fix.

**The forced consequence: `PICKER_WINDOW_SECONDS` 12 → 11.** The countdown ends at `Playing` entry, so the runway between the picker closing and the phase ending must be at least the sequence's length: `3.05 s` needed against the `15 - 12 = 3.0 s` a twelve-second window leaves — the first caption would have appeared **three frames before the panel closed**. Eleven leaves four, so the sequence fits with **0.95 s** of frozen belt in front of it, which is the same breath the twelve-second window had against the shorter countdown. The picker gave up a second so the countdown could have one; the pause between them did not move. `tuning.ts`'s docblock that argued for twelve is rewritten in place, including the arithmetic and the fact that the constraint is now `PICKER_WINDOW_SECONDS + countdownLength <= WAITING_SECONDS`.

**Audit.** Changed: `src/client/controllers/countdown-controller.ts` (three constants and their docblocks, plus a class-docblock section recording why the alignment was declined), `src/shared/tuning.ts` (`PICKER_WINDOW_SECONDS` and its docblock), `README.md` (two "12 s" citations). Build exit 0, lint 0 problems, prettier clean, `\uXXXX` zero, `flamework.build` unchanged at **29 identifiers**. **`npm test` not run.**

**Placeholders:** `CAPTION_IN_SECONDS` (0.4), `CAPTION_OUT_SECONDS` (0.2), `SCALE_INCOMING` (2.7), `PICKER_WINDOW_SECONDS` (11). `SCALE_SWEPT` (1.85), `START_HOLD_SECONDS` (0.6), `START_FADE_SECONDS` (0.25), `TEXT_SIZE` (144) and the box are unchanged.

**Studio-only:** whether 3.05 s reads as a count rather than a rush (the number to move next is `CAPTION_IN_SECONDS`, then `START_HOLD_SECONDS`); whether `Start!` now feels clipped at the end, since it is the one caption that did not get longer and it now follows three slower ones — the brief said to leave it unless the end reads clipped, and that judgement needs a screen; whether a `2.7` incoming still reads as motion at all rather than as a pop; and whether eleven seconds is long enough to read three cards and click (nothing measures that yet — the timeout pick is the only evidence).

## 153. The sway had one period for the whole belt, and a phase draw is only spread *on average*

**Reported, second time: "the sways look very syncized. Not enough randomness in the timing."** The phases were drawn correctly — item 151's line proves it — so the complaint was about the model, not the draw. Two separate reasons, and the field needed both fixed.

**1. Every ball shared one period, so the field could never change arrangement.** `swayOmega` was hoisted once per tick from `SWAY_FREQUENCY_HZ` and every ball used it. A phase offset between two equal-period sines is *constant forever*: whatever spread the draw produced on the spawn tick is the spread the field has for the whole round. That is a still picture of offsets viewed at a moving instant, and it reads as one mechanism however well the phases are spread. **`SWAY_FREQUENCY_JITTER = 0.3`** now gives each ball its own rate, drawn once at spawn (`omega` on the `lateral` state, stored in rad/s so the tick does no per-ball arithmetic), so periods run `7.7 s` to `14.3 s`. Two balls at opposite ends of that range drift through a **complete relative cycle in ~17 s**, so the arrangement never repeats within a ride. `0` restores item 107 exactly.

**2. The phase draw was not the problem, but the sample was.** The log that prompted this is worth reading as data. Round one: `2.907, 1.023, 2.854, 1.982, 1.081, 2.654, 2.529` — seven balls inside `1.02 .. 2.91` of a possible `0 .. 3.14`, with two pairs within `0.06 rad`. Normalised, the field spanned **0.60 of π ≈ 3 s of a 10 s cycle**, i.e. every ball doing the same thing inside a three-second window. Nothing was wrong with `math.random`; that is an ordinary sample. The eye never sees the distribution, it sees the sample.

So the phase is now a **golden-ratio stride with a random rotation per spawn** rather than an independent draw: `phase = ((random() + n · (sqrt(5)-1)/2) mod 1) · SWAY_PHASE_JITTER`, where `n` is a session counter (`swaySpawns`, advanced across rounds so a lane does not get a fixed phase). Measured over 40,000 trials of seven balls:

| spread, as a fraction of `π` | min | p1 | p5 | median |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| uniform draw | 0.10 | 0.35 | 0.48 | 0.77 |
| golden stride | **0.76** | 0.76 | 0.76 | 0.85 |

The stride's *worst case* beats the draw's *first percentile*, and the round that was reported scored 0.60 — below the stride's floor. The trade is named in the docblock: each ball's phase is individually less random, and the field is more independent, which is the direction the complaint asks for.

**The log now carries the period beside the phase** — `sway=2.907@9.87s,1.023@12.4s,…` — because the pair is what decides whether two balls drift apart or stay the offset they were drawn with. Identical periods beside different phases would name this defect directly.

**Audit.** Changed: `src/shared/tuning.ts` (`SWAY_FREQUENCY_JITTER` added; `SWAY_FREQUENCY_HZ`'s docblock now says it is the base rate), `src/server/services/ball-spawner-service.ts` (the `lateral` state gains `omega`, `swaySpawns`, `newSway` rewritten, `stepBallSpeeds` uses the per-ball rate, round-start line prints phase@period). Build exit 0, lint 0 problems, prettier clean, `\uXXXX` zero, `flamework.build` unchanged at **29 identifiers**. **`npm test` not run.**

**Placeholders:** `SWAY_FREQUENCY_JITTER` (0.3). Unchanged: `SWAY_FREQUENCY_HZ` (0.1), `SWAY_AMPLITUDE` (2), `SWAY_PHASE_JITTER` (`pi`), `SWAY_TRACK_SECONDS` (1.5). The golden-ratio stride is derived (`(sqrt(5)-1)/2`), not tuned.

**Studio-only:** whether a field of drifting periods reads as independent rather than as "out of time with each other" — a very wide jitter can look like a bug rather than as life, and `0.3` is a guess; whether the corrected sway still reads at all after item 151 removed the resonance amplification (the amplitude question left open there is untouched); and whether the phase stride's guaranteed spread looks *too* even — a low-discrepancy sequence is, by construction, more regular than dice, and if the field reads as evenly spaced rather than as random the answer is a little noise added to the stride, not a return to the draw.

## 154. The coin is the user's icon at three sites, and the fade driver had to learn about images

**Extends items 58 (the `colors.coin` domain slot), 71 (the picker's re-roll cost row), 132/133 (the payout panel's coin and its outline decision) and 144 (the "image did not load" boot check).** Does not touch any price, label, `COIN_SIZE` (still 20 px), the store's or the payout's layout, or any VFX.

**There were three coin sites, not two, and the picker was not one of them.** The brief named the store, the payout panel and the picker. The real set is the **store** (`coinDot`, two call sites — the header pill and every chest price row), the **payout panel** (`coinDot`, the balance plate) and the **reward toast** (an inline coin beside the granted amount), which the brief did not mention at all. The **picker draws no coin**: its re-roll cost row is a 10 px square `Frame` rotated 45° with a 1 px `UICorner` — a *diamond*, not a disc, at `DIAMOND_SIZE` rather than `COIN_SIZE` — plus a `colors.coin` label. It was left alone, and that is the one judgement call in this round: replacing it would be inventing a change the brief forbids, and a 20 px icon in a 10 px slot would be a layout change. **If the user wants it, it is one line** — `DIAMOND_SIZE`/`DIAMOND_ROTATION` give way to an `ImageLabel` at `COIN_ICON_ASSET_ID` scaled to whatever that row wants.

**`shared/ui/coin.ts` owns the id, the URI and the check.** `COIN_ICON_ASSET_ID = "128573978747266"` (the user's upload, like the hit sound and pickup sprite ids — **not** a `Placeholder.`), `coinIconUri()` builds `rbxassetid://…`, and `reportCoinIconLoad()` preloads once. **The constant did not go in `tuning.ts`**, which the brief recommended: that file exports values and **no functions** — a property a reader relies on when scanning it for "what can I retune" — and the coin needs an id, a builder and a preload. `sounds.config.ts` is the closer precedent (`SOUND_TUNING` + `soundUri`), and this is its image analogue.

**The bare id would not have rendered.** The brief asked to verify whether `Image = "<bare id>"` resolves; the tree's working code says no — `PickupSpriteController` returns `` `rbxassetid://${PICKUP_SPRITE_ASSET_ID}` `` with the measured comment *"a bare number loads nothing and reports no error"*, and `BELT_TEXTURE_ASSET` carries its prefix inside the constant. This follows the pickup sprite: bare constant, one builder, prefixed at the single point of use.

**The stroke split is now deliberate and stated at all three sites.** Store: **none**, unchanged — it sits inside a saturated price pill where an edge was removed on purpose (item 58), and an icon carries its own. Payout: **keeps** its 2 px `colors.shadow` — it sits on a charcoal plate beside the largest number on screen, which is the argument item 133 made for it. Toast: **keeps** its `CHUNKY_CONTROL_OUTLINE` edge. All three now say why in place, so the next round cannot read "one has a stroke and one does not" as an oversight. The `UICorner` is gone everywhere: an image is its own shape and a corner radius would clip it.

**The bug this round had to fix: `ImageTransparency` is not `BackgroundTransparency`.** Both the payout panel and the toast fade their contents through a `reveal` `NumberValue` whose `paint` sets `BackgroundTransparency` on every non-`TextLabel` in `faded`. The coin was in that array. As an `ImageLabel` its background is already transparent, so the fade would have moved a box with nothing in it and left **the picture at full opacity on the first frame** — a coin appearing a quarter-second before the panel it belongs to, and never fading out. Both drivers now branch three ways (`ImageLabel` → `ImageTransparency`, `TextLabel` → `TextTransparency`, else → `BackgroundTransparency`), and both coins are built at `ImageTransparency = 1`.

**One `[Coin]` line per session, not three.** `reportCoinIconLoad()` is guarded by a module flag and called from all three `onStart`s, so three controllers that draw one picture print one line: `[Coin] icon loaded 128573978747266`, or `… did not load … status=…` on `Failure`. The panels are built first and render either way — a missing icon is a **gap where the coin was**, not a hidden price row or a refused store, because the number beside it is the information.

**`colors.coin` is not an orphan and is not deleted.** It lost its only *fill* use (three circles), but six sites still read it for ink: the payout's total, base and bonus figures and its bonus-bar fill; the toast's amount; the picker's diamond and cost label. Its docblock is rewritten in place to say the circle is over, that the meaning is not, and that deleting the slot would push six sites onto an amber literal — the exact outcome item 58 exists to prevent.

**Audit.** New: `src/shared/ui/coin.ts`. Changed: `src/client/controllers/shop-controller.ts` (`coinDot` → `ImageLabel`, the docblock that argued for the placeholder rewritten, one `reportCoinIconLoad` call), `payout-controller.ts` (the coin, the three-way fade, the docblock, the call), `reward-toast-controller.ts` (the same three), `src/shared/ui/theme.ts` (`coin`'s docblock). Build exit 0, lint 0 problems, prettier clean, `\uXXXX` zero, `flamework.build` unchanged at **29 identifiers** (no new controller; `coin.ts` is a module). **`npm test` not run.**

**Placeholders:** none invented. `COIN_ICON_ASSET_ID` is the user's asset; `COIN_SIZE` is untouched at 20.

**Studio-only:** whether `128573978747266` is an `Image` class the experience may render (the `[Coin]` line answers it on the next playtest); whether a detailed icon reads at **20 px** — this is the likeliest follow-up, and the fix would be raising `COIN_SIZE` in all three files, not changing the asset; whether a `UIStroke` on a 20 px icon muddies it where it clarified a flat circle (if so the payout keeps its shadow and the toast drops to no edge, which is a per-site call); and whether the icon reads as "the same coin" beside the payout's much larger figure than it did as a flat disc.

## 155. The prize shelf expands into a read-only catalog, as a second state of the same sheet

**Extends items 55/57/58/59/61/62 (the store's hierarchy and its constants), 63 (the deleted tabs and the `View All` placeholder this round finishes), 112–123 (the chunky builders and item 118's one-stroke lesson), 144–147 (the shelf and the "a missing image draws nothing" precedent) and 154 (the coin icon, untouched here).** Touches no purchase path, no policy gate, no `busy` guard, no economy table, no rail, no picker, no inventory, no payout panel and no VFX.

**Two entry points, one destination, and both had to be built.** The `View All` label was the placeholder item 63 left behind — *"a label rather than a button so nothing invites a click that would do nothing"* — and that reasoning inverted the moment there was somewhere to go, so it is now a `TextButton` with `applyChunkyChrome`. The shelf cards were `Frame`s and are now `TextButton`s with the same chrome, because a card that opens a view is a control. The comment that argued for each of the old shapes is rewritten in place in both places.

**The view is a sibling band of `Content` inside the store's own vertical list**, hidden until asked for. The header, the coin pill and the close button are therefore *the same objects* in both states rather than a copy — which is the whole reason it is a second state and not a second sheet. `expandedChest` is the entire state, and `Back` clears it.

**`View All` lives in both chest sections, so the view takes a `ChestSpec` rather than assuming the coin chest.** `chestSpecOf(kind)` returns `{kind, title, rarities, weights, odds}`: `RARITIES` + `RARITY_WEIGHTS` + `chestOdds()` for the coin chest, `ROBUX_CHEST_RARITIES` + `robuxChestWeights()` + `robuxChestOdds()` for the paid one. A `View All` that did nothing in the Premium section would have been the same placeholder bug in the other column.

**Per-ball probability is a derivation, and it was checked by running it.** One ball's chance is `weights[rarity] / sum(weights) * 100 / BALL_POOL[rarity].size()`, at the odds module's one-decimal rounding. Shipped values, computed outside the engine:

| chest | common | rare | epic | legendary | items |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| coin | 15% ×4 | 15% ×2 | 4.5% ×2 | 0.5% ×2 | **10** |
| premium | — | 32.5% ×2 | 12.5% ×2 | 5% ×2 | **6** |

Both columns sum to 100.00%. The count is `BALL_POOL`'s own, so a new ball adds a card and changes the "<N> items" line with no code change.

**The grid's columns are derived, not chosen.** `UIGridLayout` fills from its container: at the sheet's 880-pixel maximum the inner width is 856, the grid's padding takes it to 848, and 96-pixel cards on 4-pixel gaps give **8 columns**. Ten cards is two rows of 104 pixels — 208 in total — inside a grid that is 302 pixels tall at a 720-pixel viewport, so on a desktop the catalog is fully visible and the scroll is a safety net for short windows rather than the normal path.

**The grid's height is a number, and that is the one place item 59's lesson could have been undone.** The sheet and its face both measure their own content; a self-sizing grid would have grown the sheet past `capToViewport`'s clamp, and because the face has `clipsDescendants = false` the overflow would have been *drawn outside the frame* rather than scrolled. `PRIZE_GRID_VIEWPORT_FRACTION` (0.42, bounded 180–340) gives the grid a box and re-applies it from the viewport watcher that already re-lays the chest row — one watcher, two answers to "how big is the screen".

**Idempotent clicks come from the destination, not the source.** The shelf is filled twice so its auto-scroll can wrap (item 58), so every card exists twice; rather than making one copy unclickable — two kinds of card in one shelf, and the seam moves as the canvas scrolls — `showPrizeView` returns immediately if that chest is already expanded.

**Deliberately not copied from the reference:** the category row (item 63 deleted `STORE_TABS`; the store is one hierarchy under a `Shop`/`Inventory` rail), the second header, and the `Open 1`/`Open 10` footer. The footer is the load-bearing omission — duplicating the purchase buttons would mean a second call site for the same remotes, a second `busy` guard and a second policy gate, so **the catalog is read-only and the player backs out to buy**.

**Physics of the layout, stated because two of them change sizes.** The shelf card's *cell* grew by `CHUNKY_CONTROL_DEPTH` (6 px) so its face keeps the old inner height — a cell of the old height would have given the face six pixels less than the art plus the name needed, and the name, drawn above the art, would have clipped it. `PRIZE_HEADER_HEIGHT` went 22 → 28 because a 22-pixel band cannot hold a chunky control whose depth satisfies `D >= 2X` and still leave a face for a label; the placeholder row grew by six when it became pressable.

**Audit.** Changed: `src/client/controllers/shop-controller.ts` only — eight constants, `ChestKind`/`ChestSpec`, nine state fields, `buildPrizeView` + `buildPrizeBackRow` + `buildPrizeChestBand` + `buildPrizeTitleBand` + `buildPrizeGrid` + `applyPrizeGridHeight` + `chestSpecOf` + `perBallPercent` + `formatPercent` + `showPrizeView` + `backToChests` + `fillPrizeView` + `buildPrizeCatalogCard`, the rewritten `buildPrizeHeaderRow`/`buildPrizeCard`/`fillPrizeShelf`, the shelf driver's gate, one extra call in the viewport watcher, and the hierarchy diagram. Build exit 0, lint 0 problems, prettier clean, `\uXXXX` zero, `grep fromHex` on the file **0**, `flamework.build` unchanged at **29 identifiers**. **`npm test` not run.**

**Placeholders:** `PRIZE_HEADER_HEIGHT` (28), `VIEW_ALL_WIDTH` (96), `PRIZE_GRID_VIEWPORT_FRACTION` (0.42), `PRIZE_GRID_MIN_HEIGHT` (180), `PRIZE_GRID_MAX_HEIGHT` (340), `PRIZE_CARD_WIDTH` (96), `PRIZE_CARD_HEIGHT` (100), `PRIZE_CARD_ART` (52), `PRIZE_CHEST_BLOCK` (44), `PRIZE_BACK_HEIGHT` (28), `PRIZE_BACK_WIDTH` (88), `PRIZE_TITLE_HEIGHT` (22), `ODDS_SEPARATOR`. Not placeholders: `BALL_POOL`, `RARITY_WEIGHTS`, the chest costs and product ids.

**Studio-only:** whether the grid scrolls inside the sheet rather than pushing it (the arithmetic says it fits at 720p; a 400-pixel window is the case to check); whether ten cards at eight columns reads as a catalog or as a shelf with two orphans in the last row; whether `Back` is discoverable at the top-left of a sheet whose close button is top-right — the two are now the same control shape, which could read as two ways to leave; whether the tinted `CHEST` block at 44 px still reads as a chest rather than as a coloured square with a word in it; and whether the rarity-coloured probability text at `overline` size is legible on charcoal, since it is the smallest text in the sheet.

## 156. The round song fades in with the countdown, not after it

**Reported: "the fade in for 'playing' phase should start at same time as countdown. Right now it is silent until countdown ends. Its odd."** Confirmed in one line of the log: `[Countdown] caption=3 remaining=3.04s` at `20:41:22.767` and `[RoundSong] play phase=Playing` at `20:41:25.851` — three seconds of countdown with no music, then a two-second ramp occupying the first two seconds of the race. **The moment the music is for was the quietest moment of the round.**

**The fix is one lead, measured from the same deadline the countdown uses.** `RoundSongController` now reads `ReplicatedStorage.PlayingDeadline` (item 149's published value), ticks on `Heartbeat`, and starts the sound when `deadline - now <= SONG_LEAD_SECONDS`. `SONG_LEAD_SECONDS = max(COUNTDOWN_SECONDS, SONG_FADE_SECONDS)` — at the shipped numbers `max(3.05, 2) = 3.05`, so the ramp begins on the same frame as the `3` and is at full volume about a second before `Start!`. The `max` is the interesting part: raising the fade past the countdown pulls the lead with it rather than leaving the ramp still climbing at the gun.

**`COUNTDOWN_SECONDS` moved to `shared/ui/countdown.ts` rather than being copied.** Two files now start something at the same instant, and "the same instant" is `PlayingDeadline - COUNTDOWN_SECONDS`. A private copy of that sum in the song controller would agree only until somebody retuned one of the four durations and not the other — so the four `Placeholder.` durations, `COUNTDOWN_TIMING` and the derived `COUNTDOWN_SECONDS` now live in the shared module beside the sequence they describe, and both controllers import them. `CountdownController` keeps only its *look* — the scale, the easing, the colours, the type. Verified after the move by compiling the module standalone and running it: total still `3.0500 s`, nine steps, last step `Start!/fade` ending at `3.0500`.

**`Playing` adopts the lead-in instead of restarting it.** `apply(PHASE_PLAYING)` used to call `restart()` unconditionally, which would have destroyed the very ramp the lead had just started — the reported bug reintroduced one branch later. A `leadArmed` flag, set only by `startLead` and cleared by the first `Playing` that survives it, is the whole of the difference: armed → adopt and log; not armed → restart, so `Playing -> Playing` (debug key `3`) still cross-restarts. The flag is also cleared on `PostGame`, `Intermission` and `Waiting`, so an abandoned lead cannot leave it armed for the next round.

**A client that joins mid-countdown still hears it.** The tick starts the sound whenever it finds `Waiting` inside the lead window, so a joiner gets the fade-in from that frame — the same "join at the point the clock says" property the countdown itself has. A joiner inside the *last* second gets a sound that is still ramping at the gun, which is the one case the `max` above cannot fix (there is no earlier moment available to it) and is accepted rather than special-cased.

**New log lines.** `mounted … lead=3.05s` · `[RoundSong] lead-in phase=Waiting remaining=<n>s lead=<n>s fade=<n>s volume=<n>` (the `remaining` is what separates "watched the whole lead-in" from "joined late") · `[RoundSong] adopt phase=Playing (lead-in already playing)`. The `play phase=Playing` line is now only printed on the restart path, so the two arrivals are distinguishable in a log by their first word.

**Audit.** Changed: `src/shared/ui/countdown.ts` (the four durations, `COUNTDOWN_TIMING` and `COUNTDOWN_SECONDS` now exported here), `src/client/controllers/countdown-controller.ts` (imports them; the timing block replaced by a pointer), `src/client/controllers/round-song-controller.ts` (the deadline read, `SONG_LEAD_SECONDS`, `tickLead`/`startLead`, `leadArmed`, the adopted branch, three log lines, the class docblock's "why `Playing`-only" section rewritten to "why it starts before `Playing`"), `README.md` (one line). Build exit 0, lint 0 problems, prettier clean, `\uXXXX` zero, `flamework.build` unchanged at **29 identifiers**. **`npm test` not run.**

**Placeholders:** none added. `SONG_LEAD_SECONDS` is derived, not tuned; the four countdown durations keep their item-152 values.

**Studio-only:** whether the song is *audible* at `Start!` rather than merely at full volume in the mixer (a 0.15 bed may still read as "starting" the moment the belt moves, and the knob for that is `SOUND_TUNING`'s volume, not the lead); whether a song that begins during the countdown competes with the countdown's own read (no sound, but attention is finite); whether the 0.15 bed over a still belt sounds like an intro or like a mistake, which is a judgement only a playtest can make; and whether a joiner inside the last second of `Waiting` perceives a half-ramped song as broken.

## 157. The lobby song plays across `Intermission` and `Waiting`, starting somewhere in the middle

**Reported: no music between rounds.** `Intermission` and `Waiting` were silent apart from UI sounds and the round song, and the user has two uploads (`103226688466405`, `139466974097755`) that should be a bed over both. One clip per `Intermission` at random, started at a random offset so repeated rounds are not the same opening, fading in over three seconds and out over three, and **never heard during the race**.

**The loop rule is three rules, and only one of them is a loop.** The loop's end is `TimeLength - 5`: the clip's tail is cut because an upload's last seconds are usually the author's own fade and splicing onto that reads as damage. The loop's start is `0`, **not** the random start: the first pass runs `start -> ceiling` and every pass after it runs `0 -> ceiling -> 0`, so the opening is heard on every loop and only the first pass is randomised. And the first pass is at least `10` seconds (`start <= ceiling - 10`), because a clip opened two seconds before its ceiling is a stutter rather than a variation.

**`song.ts` is parameterised, with the round song's two constants as the defaults.** The loop points were **not** parameters — `songWrapTarget(timePosition)` closed over `SONG_END_SECONDS`/`SONG_INTRO_END_SECONDS`, and `createSongHandle()` hard-coded the asset id, the fade length and `TimePosition = 0` in `play()`. It is now `songWrapTarget(timePosition, loopEnd = SONG_END_SECONDS, loopStart = SONG_INTRO_END_SECONDS)`, `createSongHandle(options?: SongOptions)` carrying `{ assetId, fadeSeconds, loopStart, loopEnd }` all defaulted to the round song's values, `play(startPosition = 0)`, and a new `setLoopPoints(start, end)` for the lobby's ceiling, which is `TimeLength - 5` and therefore only knowable **after** the clip loads. The sibling `lobbySong.ts` the brief allowed was the fallback and was not needed: the two songs differ in four numbers, and everything they share (the fade tween, the wrap, the one `RenderStepped` connection and its one disconnect site, the `started` gate that stops a pending load being read as a finished sound) is the part that must not exist twice.

**`RoundSong`'s behaviour is byte-identical, and `song.spec.ts` is untouched.** Every case in that spec calls `songWrapTarget` with **one** argument, so the defaults reproduce the closed-over constants exactly; the file did not have to change, which is the proof rather than a claim about it. The round controller's call sites are also unchanged — `createSongHandle()` bare and `handle.play()` bare. The one behavioural edit on the shared path is the **order** inside `play()`: it used to write `TimePosition = 0` then `Volume = 0` then `Play()`, and now writes `Volume = 0`, `Play()`, then `TimePosition = startPosition`. For the round song that is `TimePosition = 0` after `Play()` instead of before, which lands the playhead in the same place; for the lobby it is the difference between a random start and a start of `0`, because `seekToLoopStart` already documents that this engine may reset the playhead on `Play()` and the last write has to win.

**`drawLobbyStart` lives in a new `src/shared/ui/lobby-song.ts`, and it is pure.** Signature: `drawLobbyStart(lengthSeconds, tailCutoffSeconds, minSpanSeconds, random) => { start, ceiling } | undefined`. It imports nothing — not the `Sound`, not `TimeLength`, not `math.random` — so `lobby-song.spec.ts` asserts it against literals with an injected `random`, the item 60/139 precedent. `ceiling = length - tailCutoff`, `maxStart = ceiling - minSpan`, **`maxStart <= 0` refuses** (the clip cannot satisfy both rules, so the caller skips and logs rather than playing something that breaks one of them), otherwise `start = clamp(random() * maxStart, 0, maxStart)`. The clamp is inside the function rather than in the caller's good behaviour: Luau's `math.random()` is `[0, 1)` but the parameter is any `() => number`, and a `math.random(0, n)`-shaped closure returns `1` about `1/(n+1)` of the time — one round in a hundred starting past the ceiling, on a boundary only the loop would notice. Its sibling `pickLobbySong(assetIds, random)` is there for the same reason and clamps its index for the same class of reason.

**The spec pins the three boundaries the brief names, and one more it is shaped around.** `start = maxStart` yields exactly `minSpan` (`55 - 45 = 10`, stated on integers because `a - (a - b)` is only exact in binary floating point where the subtraction does not round — the first draft used `15.02` and the standalone run returned `0.019999999999999574`, so the case now uses `15.5`); a length of `tailCutoff + minSpan - 0.001` is refused; a sweep of `random` values from `-0.25` to `1.5` never draws past `maxStart` or below `0`; and **`drawLobbyStart(0, …)` refuses**, which is the unloaded clip. A clip of exactly `tailCutoff + minSpan` is refused too, deliberately: a zero-width range is a "random" start that is always the same one. Verified by compiling `lobby-song.ts` standalone with `tsc` and running every assertion under `node` — all pass, and 5,000 draws over a 213 s clip spread `0.01 … 197.94` against a `198` maximum.

**The `Loaded` wait is `IsLoaded`/`TimeLength` first, then `Sound.Loaded`, then a 0.1 s poll up to `LOBBY_LOAD_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`.** `song.ts` gates both the frame wrap and the `Ended` handler on `play()` having been called, so the handle exists but does nothing until the controller is ready — which is what makes the wait possible at all. The readiness test is `sound.IsLoaded || sound.TimeLength > 0`, asked **before** the event is connected (for a fetched asset the event fired long ago, and subscribing alone to a latch that is already set would hang on the common path rather than the rare one), and the poll exists because an event that never fires and a length that never arrives fail identically. On expiry the id is marked unusable, the handle is destroyed, and **the other clip is tried immediately inside the same `Intermission`** rather than the lobby staying silent until the next one — with two songs that recursion is at most two deep and the second attempt prints the single `no asset loaded` line. `INTERMISSION_SECONDS` is 30, so even the worst case (both clips timing out) fits inside one lobby phase.

**The `generation` guard, and the debug sequence that would catch a missing check.** `generation` is bumped **first** in `beginSong`, before the old handle is destroyed, so the bump invalidates any in-flight `Loaded` wait or fade completion belonging to the outgoing song; every continuation captures it and returns if it has moved, and the belt beside it is `this.song === handle`. The catching sequence is `PostGame -> Intermission -> Waiting` three times inside a second — three `Intermission` entries, three picks, three handles. Without the bump, entry two's `Loaded` callback starts a song into entry three's handle, and entry one's fade completion clears `this.song` while a live handle sits in it; the log would show `play generation=2` after `fade-out generation=3` and `start=` on a clip nobody picked.

**`Waiting` is a no-op branch that returns immediately, and that is the requirement.** The two phases are one continuous lobby and every re-entry point is a place a restart could hide; the only ways to be sure none of them happens is for the phase to have no code. The two things that may touch the song during `Waiting` are named: the fade-out timer and the `Playing` safety net.

**A mid-`Waiting` joiner hears the same `0 -> ceiling` pass as everyone else, after their own random first pass.** `onStart` seeds from the current phase value, so a client joining during `Intermission` **or** `Waiting` starts a song rather than sitting silent until the next round — the same "join at the point the clock says" property the countdown and the round song have. Their pick and their start are their own (both are per-client by design), so their *first* pass differs from the client who watched the `Intermission` entry; from the moment the loop wraps, both are playing `0 -> ceiling -> 0` and are therefore in the same place. That wrap is the reason the joiner question has no sharp edge here.

**The fade-out is timed off `PlayingDeadline`, and a deadline of `0` is "not known yet", not "now".** `tickFade` computes `deadline - GetServerTimeNow()` on `Heartbeat` and starts the fade when it is within `LOBBY_SONG_FADE_SECONDS` — measured rather than counted down, so a dropped frame or a late joiner still lands the fade three seconds before the gun. **The brief said to fade immediately when the deadline is `0`, and that is wrong**: `enterWaiting` calls `publishPhase()` *before* `publishPlayingDeadline(endsAt)`, so a client can legitimately observe `Waiting` while the value still holds the previous round's `0`. Fading on that would silence the lobby for the whole of `Waiting`, which is the opposite of the item. The `Playing` entry is the safety net for a deadline that never arrives: it starts the fade immediately if it has not already, and is a no-op if it has.

**The `PostGame` decision is destroy-immediately.** There is no fade to let finish — `Playing` took the song out three seconds before — and a `PostGame` reached straight from `Waiting` is a lobby that was abandoned rather than a race that finished, so a musical tail would be sound for a round that never happened. Every other unrecognised phase destroys too.

**The two volumes are `0.1` each, below the round song's `0.15`.** Two thirds of the bed level a race gets, because the lobby is where a player reads the store, the prize view and the countdown, and a bed at a race's level makes those panels feel like they are shouting over the music. **Two rows rather than one shared `LOBBY_SONG_VOLUME`**, even though the numbers are equal: the two clips are the user's own uploads and their relative loudness is not knowable from here (an upload normalised at -14 LUFS and one at -8 are nine decibels apart and nothing in the repository can measure it), so the first person to listen must be able to move one without the other. `playbackSpeed: 1` on both is load-bearing rather than tidy — it rescales wall-clock time, and the ceiling is derived from `TimeLength`, which does not rescale, so a pitched clip would loop five *pitched* seconds from its end.

**The boot check is one `ContentProvider.PreloadAsync` for both ids, and it decides nothing.** The first version of this round used the fetch status as a gate: a `Failure` removed the id from the picker, two `Failure`s printed `no asset loaded, silent` and disabled the controller for the session. **The first Studio run silenced the lobby completely**, and the log showed why the gate was wrong:

```
ContentId: rbxassetid://103226688466405 failed due to: Asset type does not match requested type
ContentId: rbxassetid://139466974097755 failed due to: Asset type does not match requested type
ContentId: rbxassetid://135266450823195 failed due to: Asset type does not match requested type
[PickupSprite] image did not load: rbxassetid://135266450823195 status=Enum.AssetFetchStatus.Failure
```

The third id is the **pickup sprite**, and `economy.roblox.com/v2/assets/135266450823195/details` reports `AssetTypeId: 1` — it is an image, used as an image, failing identically to two audio assets whose `AssetTypeId` is `3` (`jojo-lobby-music` and `kulovka-lobby-2`, both owned by creator `prospeed1`, the account whose data store logged `coins=73297`). A check that fails the same way for correct and incorrect content is not measuring the content, and the same verdict was already on record for the coin icon (item 154) and the pickup sprite (item 144) — both of which kept drawing. Items 144 and 154 both concluded *report it and render it anyway*; this controller made the same signal behaviour-changing and paid for it with a silent lobby.

So the preload is now a **diagnostic and a cache warmer only**: one `did not load <id>` line per id it dislikes, one `preload done liked=<n> disliked=<n>` summary, and no effect on the pick. `no asset loaded, silent` is now reachable only when a `Sound` itself never reports a length within ten seconds — a measurement of the thing being asked to play, not an opinion about it. Same precedent, same file, one round late.

**New log lines.** `[LobbySong] mounted fade=3s tailCutoff=5s minSpan=10s assets=<A>|<B> volume=<a>/<b>` · `[LobbySong] asset did not load <id> status=<…> (a preload opinion, not a verdict)` · `[LobbySong] preload done liked=<n> disliked=<n> of 2` · `[LobbySong] play song=<id> start=<s>s ceiling=<s>s length=<s>s loopStart=0 generation=<n> endsAt=<n>` (the `length` is what proves the clip really loaded, and it is the number the draw was bounded by) · `[LobbySong] skipped song=<id> reason=too-short length=<s> (needs more than <n>s)` · `[LobbySong] skipped song=<id> reason=not-loaded after <n>s (IsLoaded=<bool>, TimeLength=<n>)` — the one line that means it · `[LobbySong] fade-out generation=<n> (<reason>, deadline=<n>, started <n>s early | <n>s late | unknown)` · `[LobbySong] destroyed generation=<n>` · `[LobbySong] no asset loaded, silent`. The fade line speaks in words rather than a signed number because `started -1.2s early` is a sentence nobody parses correctly, and "late" is a dropped-frame report rather than a detail.

**Audit.** Added: `src/shared/ui/lobby-song.ts`, `src/shared/ui/lobby-song.spec.ts`, `src/client/controllers/lobby-song-controller.ts`. Changed: `src/shared/sounds.config.ts` (two ids, `LOBBY_SONG_ASSET_IDS`, three durations, two `SOUND_TUNING` rows, the row count in `SOUND_TUNING`'s docblock), `src/shared/sounds.config.spec.ts` (two ids in `ALL_IDS`, "seven" → "nine" in two titles, one new `it` for the lobby rows), `src/shared/ui/song.ts` (`SongOptions`, `setLoopPoints`, `play(startPosition)`, the three-parameter `songWrapTarget`, four docblocks rewritten in place — the module header, the loop section, `songWrapTarget`'s parameter section and the `Ended` comment), `README.md` (the audio paragraph and the controller count). **After the first Studio run**, `src/client/controllers/lobby-song-controller.ts` lost `available`/`assetsKnown`/`resumeIfWanted` and gained `unusable`/`pickable`/`giveUp`, a 0.1 s readiness poll and the `length=` field on the play line — the controller was 640 lines of correct design around one wrong premise, and the premise was the preload. Build exit 0, lint 0 problems, prettier clean, `\uXXXX` zero in `src`, `flamework.build` regenerated from a deleted copy and now **30 identifiers** (was 29). **`npm test` not run.** Untouched: `RoundSongController`, the picker, the countdown, the transition wipe and the phase machine — no remote, no attribute, no server work.

**Placeholders:** `LOBBY_SONG_FADE_SECONDS = 3`; `LOBBY_SONG_TAIL_CUTOFF_SECONDS = 5`; `LOBBY_SONG_MIN_SPAN_SECONDS = 10`; `LOBBY_SONG_A_ASSET_ID` volume `0.1`; `LOBBY_SONG_B_ASSET_ID` volume `0.1`; `LOBBY_LOAD_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 10`; `LOBBY_LOAD_POLL_SECONDS = 0.1`. The two asset ids are the user's uploads and are **not** placeholders; both are `AssetTypeId: 3` (audio) on the catalog, verified out of band.

**Studio-only:** whether either id actually plays — the **first** Studio run says the preload dislikes both and cannot say more than that, so the answering line is now `play song=… length=<s>s` (it loaded and is playing) or `skipped song=… reason=not-loaded (IsLoaded=…, TimeLength=…)` (it did not); whether a random start reads as a mid-phrase entry or as a bug — the offset is uniform and this repository cannot know where a clip's phrases are; whether the wrap `ceiling -> 0` is seamless on the engine's `TimePosition`, which decides whether item 139's arithmetic is enough or whether `Sound.LoopRegion` (still untested, still named in `song.ts`) is the successor; whether a three-second fade at a mid-phrase start reads as intentional; and whether a joiner's `0 -> ceiling` pass beside another client's mid-`start` first pass is noticeable, which is the one consequence of per-client randomness that two testers in one server will hear.

## 158. If the picked lobby song is unavailable, the other one plays

**Asked: "if `103226688466405` is unavailable, use the song `139466974097755`."** The fallback existed in item 157's code but only for one of the two failure kinds and only at one attempt's worth of patience: a clip that loaded and was *too short* was retired without retrying, and the timeout was a fixed ten seconds per attempt, so a lobby with two dead ids spent twenty seconds — most of an `Intermission` — proving it. Both are fixed.

**Two failure kinds, one path.** `retire(handle, pick, generation)` is now the only way an attempt ends badly: it marks the id `unusable` for the session, records it in `failedThisLobby`, destroys the handle, and calls `start` again. A clip that never reports a length and a clip that reports nine seconds both arrive there, differing only in the `warn` that precedes it. A lobby that fell back because its first song was silent and a lobby that fell back because its first song was too short are the same lobby: one that should be playing the other song.

**The budget had to become a budget.** `LOBBY_LOAD_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 10` per attempt became `LOBBY_LOAD_BUDGET_SECONDS = 10` per **lobby**, with `attemptSeconds(candidates)` dividing it and `LOBBY_MIN_ATTEMPT_SECONDS = 3` as the floor. Two songs get five seconds each; the fallback therefore completes inside ten seconds, against an `Intermission` of 30 and a `Waiting` of 15.

**A simulation caught the first version of that division.** Dividing by the candidates *still* pickable, recomputed per attempt, gives `5 + 10 = 15` for two dead ids — the second attempt is divided by one instead of two, so the shares grow as ids fail and the "budget" re-derives itself. The share is therefore computed **once, in `beginSong`**, and stored on `this.attempt`; every attempt in a lobby uses the same number. Re-simulated: `both good → play (5s)`, `A dead → skip A 5s, play B`, `both dead → skip A 5s, skip B 5s, silent` at exactly 10 s, `three ids → 3.33s each`. `attemptSeconds(0)` answers the whole budget rather than `math.huge`, which is reachable from `beginSong` and would turn a silent lobby into a permanent one.

**A dead set is not a dead session.** Both ids were uploaded minutes before this session (`Created: 2026-11-09T01:40Z` and `01:45Z` against a clock at `21:25` on the 8th), and a fresh audio asset is not necessarily servable yet.
